structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: The text is a notice from Kotak Mahindra Bank to stock exchanges regarding its 40th AGM on August 2, 2025, held via video conferencing. It submits the Integrated Annual Report 2024-25, including financial statements, Directors' and Auditors' Reports, MD&A, and BRSR, along with the AGM Notice. It details dissemination via email, QR codes, and websites. The report's theme, 'Transforming for scale,' is explained, emphasizing customer-centric transformation, principles of speed, simplicity, transparency, and technology, employee empowerment, and sustainable, responsible growth. It highlights the bank's diversified business mix and strong balance sheet as sources of resilience and long-term value creation.

nodes.title: About us
nodes.summary: Established in 1985, Kotak is a leading diversified Indian financial services conglomerate offering solutions across customer and geographic segments, including overseas subsidiaries and branches. Built on trust, governance, risk management, innovation, and entrepreneurial management, it serves long-term stakeholder interests. With assets of ₹8.8 trillion and market capitalization of ₹4.3 trillion as of March 31, 2025, it offers products across four engines—banking and lending, capital markets, asset management, and protection—for counter-cyclical benefits. Key metrics include total assets ₹879,774 crore, advances ₹486,166 crore, deposits ₹494,707 crore, AUM ₹669,885 crore, relationship value ₹920,000 crore+, 114,000+ employees, and 5.3 crore bank customers.

nodes.title: Orchestrating Cohesive User Experiences Across Multiple Platforms
nodes.summary:
Orchestrating Cohesive User Experiences Across Multiple Platforms
Our commitment to delivering a seamless customer experience across physical, digital and voice channels remains a core strategic priority. Kotak continues to play an active role in India’s digital transformation, consistently working to enhance and simplify the banking experience for its customers. The Bank is further strengthening its distribution framework across these channels, with product-led propositions aligned to defined customer personas within target segments. Our services are accessible through a diverse set of platforms including the website, mobile apps, WhatsApp, chatbots, voice bots and self-service kiosks, ensuring a consistent and convenient experience across all touchpoints.
While we will explore our digital footprint in greater detail later, it is worth noting that our digital ecosystem is supported by a resilient and scalable technology architecture. This foundation enables us to deliver agile, secure and innovative solutions to our customers, helping us stay future-ready and customer-centric.

nodes.title: Dear Shareholders,
nodes.summary: A letter to shareholders of Kotak reviewing a year of resilience, recovery, reinvention, and realignment. It covers the external context of geopolitical tensions and India's 6.5% economic growth with RBI rate cuts. Kotak-specific issues include RBI directives to strengthen technology, pause digital onboarding and credit card issuance, and the subsequent lifting of the embargo in February 2025; the microfinance downturn and operating model changes; and the strategic vision to transform for scale with technology and customer-centricity. It highlights Kotak's diversified financial conglomerate position, progress against four stakeholders (Customer, Company, Colleague, Community), customer propositions including Private Bank, 811, SME, and Solitaire, technology investments and persona-based apps (Kotak Mobile Banking, 811, Neo, Cherry, fyn), customer journey improvements, and a 28% reduction in complaints.

nodes.title: Message from Ashok Vaswani
nodes.summary: Ashok Vaswani's message emphasizes building sustainable shareholder value through prudent risk management and governance, targeting asset growth of 1.5-2x nominal GDP, with FY25 advances up 18% and deposits up 16%. Book value per share grew 21%. The Consumer Bank faced a technology embargo, the Commercial Bank was impacted by a microfinance downturn, while the Corporate Bank remained resilient and Tractor Finance achieved 11.5% market share. The diversified model provided counter-cyclical benefits, with stellar performance in capital markets, including KMCC's third consecutive #1 ECM ranking, and strong institutional equities, asset management, retail securities, and life insurance. A strong risk culture remains central. The balance sheet strength enabled the acquisition of a ₹3,330 crore personal loan book from Standard Chartered Bank, India. Colleagues are the greatest asset, with culture change initiatives like 'Best of Kotak for Kotakites,' transparent career plans, the Kotak Young Leaders programme, and new financial and non-financial senior management measures to foster customer centricity and collaboration.

nodes.title: “Over the years, our vision and aspirations have evolved to achieve the audacious.”
nodes.summary: The text outlines Kotak Mahindra Bank's vision, community commitment, and transformation journey. It emphasizes regulatory alignment, compliance, and sustainable franchise building. Community initiatives focus on financial inclusion, education, healthcare, and sustainability, including Kotak Biz Labs for entrepreneurs. It highlights the brand's evolution and partnership with aspirational India. The business overview details a customer-centric strategy, with Consumer Banking organized into Product, Distribution, and Proposition segments. Digital and voice channels, persona-driven branches, and integrated solutions like Kotak Solitaire enhance customer experience. Branch decongestion and frontline digitization improve service. Strategic outcomes include optimized deposit mix, improved cost of funds, and enhanced portfolio granularity and yield.

key_items: Leveraging Technology to Drive Customer Value and Strengthen Compliance
nodes.summary: Kotak at a Glance covers business overviews of three entities. Kotak Mahindra Prime Limited provides car and two-wheeler loans to retail consumers and dealers, plus Loan Against Property financing, offering new and pre-owned vehicle financing, wholesale dealership financing, manufacturer tie-ups, and LAP for commercial/residential real estate. It leverages technology—Aadhaar eKYC with facial recognition, data analytics, a cloud compliance platform with audit tools, and a LAP loan origination platform—to enhance customer value and compliance. Kotak Mahindra Investments Limited focuses on real estate developer finance, corporate loans, and strategic investments, lending across residential, commercial, and retail segments and to diversified sectors like manufacturing, services, education, and NBFCs. Kotak Infrastructure Debt Fund Limited provides long-term finance (loans and NCDs) to infrastructure projects with at least one year of satisfactory commercial operations. Performance metrics: 16% YoY AUM growth and 0.14% net NPA on customer assets.

nodes.summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank's FY 2024-25 technology transformation focused on upgrading core infrastructure and app UI/UX to enhance customer experience, resolve RBI restrictions, and achieve scale. We have identified certain high value customer segments and seek to meet their needs holistically.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity and Data Privacy
nodes.summary:
Cybersecurity and Data Privacy
As technology continues to evolve and cyber threats grow in complexity, the Bank remains committed to cybersecurity and data privacy as core pillars of its IT governance framework. We believe that protection of sensitive information and assurance of uninterrupted service are critical to continue serving millions of customers across multiple digital touch-points.
Our governance framework for managing technology and cybersecurity risks is structured around a three-line defence system, as detailed below:
1st
Information Technology (IT) Team and Business Units
2nd
Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) who reports to the Head of Risk Management
3rd
Internal Audit
We have established clear controls and mechanisms to identify and address cybersecurity risks. Specifically, we have implemented controls in the following areas:
Prevention
Detection

nodes.title: Response

Detection includes 24x7 SOC, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and escalation. Response and recovery feature BCP, IT DR with RTO, and successful DR drills three times in FY 2024-25. Training programs include induction, annual refreshers, phishing awareness, and LMS courses, with ~72,000 employees completing 76,000 hours in FY 2024-25.

nodes.title: Response and Recovery
nodes.summary:
Response and Recovery
We maintain a dedicated email channel for cybersecurity concerns to support incident reporting. Our layered technology architecture, along with robust Disaster Recovery (DR) and Business Continuity Plans (BCP), enables effective management of operational risks and ensures continuity of service under all conditions.
The Bank has an IT DR plan and drill calendar which defines the frequency of DR drills for critical and non-critical applications. The IT DR Plan specifies the Recovery Time Objective (RTO). RTO is the period of time within which IT infrastructure, systems, applications and databases must be recovered at the DR site. The Bank has demonstrated its capability to move all critical and dependent business and infrastructure applications to DR site and operate from there for extended periods. This has been tested thrice in FY 2024-25.

nodes.title: Resource Management
nodes.summary: The text covers Kotak's resource management initiatives: reducing paper usage by 47 lakh A4 sheets via duplex printing and electronic statements; using recycled paper at select offices, saving 7.6 tons of virgin paper and avoiding 10.2 tCO2e emissions; and Sonata's digitization of loan processes, including e-signing and WhatsApp sharing. It also details other environmental initiatives: employee awareness sessions, EV charging stations, and Green Seal housekeeping chemicals. Finally, it outlines the ESG Policy Framework, focusing on optimizing energy and water consumption, regulatory compliance, investment in energy-efficient technologies, and increasing renewable energy reliance to minimize environmental footprint and create long-term stakeholder value.

nodes.title: Colleagues at the Core
nodes.summary: This section covers Kotak Mahindra Bank's workforce overview—including employee strength, diversity, turnover, and talent acquisition—organized around five pillars of talent engagement: Best of Kotak, transparent communication, colleague development, culture of appreciation, and value proposition. It details learning initiatives like Kotak MyLearn, leadership programmes, performance management, succession planning, diversity and inclusion, health and wellness benefits, employee volunteering, recognition, occupational health and safety, human rights, and CSR expenditure and beneficiary reach. Inclusion is addressed. The CSR report covers education and healthcare access, community resilience, flagship institutions—including the Kotak Education Foundation, sports academy, AI-ML centre, energy mission, sustainability school, and BizLabs accelerator—and diversity programs supporting people with disabilities and women entrepreneurs, highlighting key outcomes and implementing partners.

nodes.title: Colleagues at the Core (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers Kotak Mahindra Bank's workforce overview, including employee strength, diversity, turnover, and talent acquisition strategies. It details five pillars of talent engagement: Best of Kotak, transparent communication, colleague development, culture of appreciation, and value proposition. It discusses learning initiatives like Kotak MyLearn, leadership programmes, performance management, succession planning, diversity and inclusion efforts, health and wellness benefits, employee volunteering, recognition, occupational health and safety, human rights, and CSR initiatives with expenditure and beneficiary reach.

nodes.title: Institutions
nodes.summary: Kotak's CSR report covers education and healthcare access, community resilience, flagship institutions, and diversity/inclusion. Education initiatives include teacher training, scholarships, infrastructure upgrades, and digital learning across thousands of schools. Healthcare focuses on cancer care, mobile medical units, and hospital infrastructure. Resilience efforts address climate adaptation through water conservation, sustainable agriculture, livestock development, skill training, nano entrepreneurship, and habitat restoration. Flagship institutions include Kotak Education Foundation, sports academy, AI-ML centre, energy mission, sustainability school, and BizLabs accelerator. Diversity programs support people with disabilities and women entrepreneurs. The report highlights key outcomes and implementing partners across all initiatives.

nodes.title: Hausla hai toh ho jayega.
nodes.summary: The text presents diverse impact stories: Phulmani Devi, a 38-year-old farmer in Jharkhand, gained support for strawberry tissue culture and goats, transforming her life and farm, with income exceeding 2 lakh per annum from 2.2 acres, goats, and poultry. Sara received emergency medical aid, safe accommodation at Home Away from Home, nutritious meals, emotional support, and counselling for her mother; she completed treatment and is in follow-up. Surta Devi in Gujarat reports the first wheat cultivation due to water availability, expecting 10-15 quintals per acre. Himanshi, daughter of a printing press worker, secured a three-month internship with Jaguar Land Rover India Ltd with a monthly stipend. Soham Amiya Roy Dastidar, 26 with autism spectrum disorder, became a Multi-Purpose Facilitator at JP Morgan. Mousum, orphaned and raised by her uncle, completed a Btech from IIT Guwahati with Kotak's support and secured a software developer placement at Goldman Sachs. A 15-month-old was diagnosed with hepatoblastoma. The stories illustrate how timely support catalyses achievements and careers.

structure.title: Financial Highlights
structure.summary: The Financial Highlights section presents consolidated and standalone financial highlights for FY 2020-21 to 2024-25, covering key indicators like advances, investments, assets, profits, NIM, ROA, book value, EPS, face value, ROE, capital adequacy, and NPAs. It includes market ratios (price, market cap, P/B, P/E) and notes on consolidation, including the divestment of Kotak Mahindra General Insurance. The section contains the Independent Auditor's Report with opinions, key audit matters (NPA provisioning, IT controls, revenue recognition), and internal financial controls. It provides the consolidated cash flow statement, schedules (capital, reserves, deposits, borrowings, other liabilities, cash, bank balances, investments, advances, fixed assets, other assets, contingent liabilities, interest earned/expended, operating expenses), and significant accounting policies (revenue recognition, fixed assets, employee benefits, investments, foreign currency, derivatives, advances, structured liabilities, securitisation, leases, provisions, contingent liabilities, share-based payments, taxes, segment reporting). It also covers tier II bonds, segment reporting, lease disclosures, related party disclosures, employee benefits, CSR, audit fees, contingent liabilities, and includes auditors' and directors' signatures.

nodes.title: Consolidated Financial Highlights 2024-2025
nodes.summary: The text presents financial highlights for FY 2020-21 through FY 2024-25, covering key financial indicators such as advances, investments, total assets, net profit, net interest margin, return on average assets, book value per share, basic earnings per share, face value, return on equity, capital adequacy ratio, gross and net NPA figures and ratios. It also includes market-related ratios: market price, market capitalisation, price to book ratio, and price to earnings ratio. Data is provided for both consolidated and standalone figures, with footnotes clarifying exclusions for investments and NIM calculations.

nodes.title: Standalone Financial Highlights 2024-2025
nodes.summary: The text presents standalone financial highlights for FY 2021 to FY 2025, including deposits, advances, investments, total assets, net interest income, fee income, other non-interest income, operating profit, provisions, tax, and net profit. It also lists key financial indicators such as net interest margin, cost-to-income ratio, return on average assets, fee/NII plus other income, NII/NII plus other income, capital adequacy ratio, tier I, gross NPA ratio, and net NPA ratio. A footnote details the June 2024 divestment of a 70% stake in Kotak Mahindra General Insurance to Zurich Insurance, resulting in a net gain and KGI becoming an associate.

nodes.title: Consolidation at a Glance

It includes capital and reserves figures as of March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. Additionally, it contains the Independent Auditor's Report on the Consolidated Financial Statements, covering the opinion, basis for opinion, and key audit matters, specifically the identification and provisioning against Non-Performing Assets, with relevant loan and provision amounts.

nodes.title: Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The Independent Auditor’s Report covers the audit of Kotak Mahindra Bank’s consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025, including the auditor’s opinion on true and fair view, key audit matters (NPA provisioning, IT systems and controls, revenue recognition for management fees), management and auditor responsibilities, other matters regarding subsidiaries and associates, and other legal and regulatory requirements. It includes auditor signatures and Annexure A on internal financial controls, detailing responsibilities, meaning, and inherent limitations. It presents the auditor’s opinion on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls, noting reliance on other auditors for subsidiaries and associates, and includes excerpts from audit reports of Kotak Mahindra Life Insurance and Zurich Kotak General Insurance with disclaimers. Finally, it presents the audited consolidated financial statements as of 31 March 2025, including balance sheet, profit and loss account, comparative figures, contingent liabilities, and accounting policies, with signatures and dates.

nodes.title: Independent Auditor’s Report (intro)
nodes.summary: This independent auditor's report covers the audit of Kotak Mahindra Bank's consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025. It includes the auditor's opinion that the statements give a true and fair view in accordance with applicable regulations. Key audit matters discussed are: identification and provisioning against non-performing assets (NPAs) for the bank and certain subsidiaries, IT systems and controls impacting financial reporting, and revenue recognition for management fees. The report outlines management's responsibilities, auditor's responsibilities, other matters regarding subsidiaries and associates audited by other auditors, and other legal and regulatory requirements including compliance with director remuneration, internal financial controls, pending litigations, and audit trail maintenance.

nodes.title: OVERVIEW
nodes.summary: This text provides an overview of Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited and its subsidiaries, describing the Group's diversified financial services, its establishment of an IBU in GIFT City in 2016, and its first overseas branch in DIFC, Dubai in 2019. It details the basis of consolidation, including compliance with AS-21 and AS-23, the consolidation of entities with over 50% voting rights or control, equity method for associates with 20-50% voting rights, treatment of goodwill, minority interest, and elimination of intragroup transactions. It lists subsidiaries with shareholding percentages as of March 31, 2025 and 2024, and associates with their shareholdings. It notes the exclusion of Kotak Karma Foundation from consolidation due to restrictions on fund transfers.

nodes.title: 2. ACCOUNTING METHODOLOGY AND SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES: A. ACCOUNTING METHODOLOGY
nodes.summary: The text outlines the accounting methodology and significant accounting policies for consolidated financial statements, prepared on a historical cost and accrual basis. It details compliance with Indian Accounting Standards, the Companies Act 2013, RBI and IRDAI guidelines, and GAAP. It distinguishes preparation bases for Indian and foreign subsidiaries and associates, noting adjustments to align with Indian GAAP and separate disclosure of differing accounting policies. It also references the Integrated Annual Report 2024-25 and financial statement schedules.

nodes.title: B. USE OF ESTIMATES
nodes.summary:
B. USE OF ESTIMATES
The preparation of financial statements requires the management to make estimates and assumptions in the reported amounts of assets and liabilities (including contingent liabilities) as at the date of the financial statements and the reported income and expenses during the reporting period. Management believes that the estimates used in preparation of the financial statements are prudent and reasonable. Actual results could differ from these estimates. Any revision in the accounting estimates is recognised prospectively in the current and future periods.

nodes.title: C. REVENUE RECOGNITION
key_items: a. Lending / Investing:; b. Investment Banking:
f. Asset Management and Advisory Services:
nodes.summary: The text details revenue recognition policies across six business segments: Lending/Investing covers interest income accrual methods for retail advances, investments, and discounted instruments; fees, commissions, and dividends; treatment of non-performing assets, securitization gains/losses, asset assignments, and Priority Sector Lending Certificates. Investment Banking recognizes fees upon milestone completion. Life Insurance addresses premium recognition (including unit-linked and lapsed policies), top-up contributions, policy charges, reinsurance premiums and profit commissions, and reinstatement interest. General Insurance covers interest accrual, premium recognition (net of tax, including installments and revisions), reinsurance commissions and premiums, premium received in advance, and premium deficiency. Broking includes placement fees, brokerage income from primary and secondary markets, depository fees, and securities lending fees. Asset Management and Advisory Services covers investment management fees, venture/private equity fund fees, advisory fees, portfolio advisory and management fees, distribution income from funds, and research fees.

nodes.title: D. FIXED ASSETS (PROPERTY, PLANT AND EQUIPMENT AND INTANGIBLE ASSETS)
nodes.summary: This text outlines the accounting policy for fixed assets (property, plant, equipment, and intangibles), covering initial measurement at cost less depreciation/amortization and impairment, cost components including purchase, freight, duties, site preparation, installation, and professional fees, capitalization of subsequent expenditure only if it enhances future benefits, and treatment of gains/losses on disposal as income/expense, with profit on bank premises sale appropriated to capital reserve per RBI guidelines. It details depreciation/amortization using the straight-line method on a pro-rata basis over estimated useful lives at rates equal to or higher than Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013, and lists useful lives for various asset types like premises, office equipment, computers, furniture, vehicles, ATMs, software, goodwill, membership card, and asset management rights. It also notes depreciation of used assets over residual life, full depreciation of assets costing less than ₹5,000 in the year of purchase, and includes a page number.

nodes.title: E. EMPLOYEE BENEFITS
nodes.summary: The section covers employee benefits, including defined benefit plans (Gratuity, Pension) and defined contribution plans (Provident Fund, Superannuation, NPS, DEWS), with actuarial measurement and recognition policies. It also details compensated absences and other long-term benefits. A major portion addresses investment accounting policies: classification into HTM, AFS, FVTPL (with HFT sub-category), and six groups per RBI Directions; SPPI assessment; acquisition cost (FIFO for Bank, weighted average for subsidiaries); treatment of broken period interest and transaction costs; disposal rules; short sales; valuation guidelines per RBI (including fair value hierarchy, day 1 gain/loss, impairment, and non-performing investments); repo/reverse repo accounting; and specific policies for life insurance (unit-linked and non-linked), general insurance, and other entities (AS-13). Transition date accounting under RBI Circular is also covered.

nodes.title: Employee Benefits: Defined Benefit and Defined Contribution Plans
nodes.summary: The page covers employee benefits, categorized into defined benefit and defined contribution plans. Defined benefit plans include Gratuity and Pension. Gratuity is provided per the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, with liabilities actuarially determined; some subsidiaries fund via trusts managed by life insurers, while others are unfunded. Pension applies to certain erstwhile ING Vysya Bank employees under IBA structure; the Bank contributes 10% of basic salary to a pension fund, with actuarial true-up, and plan assets are recognized. Actuarial gains/losses are immediately recognized in profit and loss. Defined contribution plans include Provident Fund, Superannuation Fund, New Pension Scheme, and DIFC Employee Workplace Savings Scheme (DEWS). Contributions are expensed when service is rendered, with no further obligations.

nodes.title: iii. Compensated Absences: Other Long-Term Employee Benefits:
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for employee benefits and investments. It details compensated absences measured actuarially using projected unit credit method with assumptions and immediate recognition of actuarial gains/losses. Other employee benefits include service awards measured actuarially and short-term benefits like performance incentives recognized when service is rendered. For investments, it outlines RBI-directed classification into HTM, AFS, and FVTPL (with HFT sub-category), further grouped into six categories. It describes settlement date accounting (except trade date for equity shares and subsidiaries), classification basis, business model assessment considering objectives, sales frequency, and risks, and the solely payments of principal and interest assessment.

nodes.title: Employee Benefits and Investment Classification Policies
nodes.summary: The page covers other employee benefits, including awards based on service years and short-term benefits like performance incentives. It then details investment policies for the Group (Bank and subsidiaries excluding insurance subsidiary) for the year ended March 31, 2025. Investment classification follows RBI Directions 2023, categorizing the portfolio into HTM, AFS, and FVTPL (with HFT as a sub-category), and further into six groups for balance sheet disclosure. It specifies settlement date accounting for securities, except trade date for equity shares by the Bank, while subsidiaries use trade date accounting. The basis of classification relies on the business model and contractual cash flow characteristics. Business model assessment considers portfolio objectives, management strategy, sales frequency and rationale, and risk management.

nodes.title: Assessment whether contractual cashflows are solely payments of principal and interest
nodes.summary: The text outlines the assessment of whether contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI), defining principal and interest and listing contractual terms considered such as reset terms, contingent events, leverage, prepayment, extension, non-recourse features, and time value modifications. It details investment classification categories: HTM (held to collect with SPPI), AFS (collect and sell with SPPI, plus irrevocable option for non-trading equity instruments), FVTPL (default for non-HTM/AFS), HFT (trading or short-term gains per RBI Circular), and a separate category for subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures. It covers acquisition cost determination (FIFO for Bank, weighted average for subsidiaries), treatment of broken period interest and transaction costs (expensed for Bank, capitalized for subsidiaries), and disposal treatment for AFS debt instruments (gain/loss from AFS Reserve to P&L) and equity instruments (gain/loss from AFS Reserve to Capital Reserve).

nodes.title: Investment Classification, Acquisition Cost, and Disposal
key_items: Investments in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures
nodes.summary: The text covers classification and accounting for investments. It details the SPPI assessment, including reset terms, contingent events, leverage, prepayment/extensions, non-recourse terms, and time value modifications. It defines HTM, AFS (with irrevocable equity option), FVTPL, and HFT (per RBI Circular) categories, plus a separate category for subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures. Acquisition cost is determined by FIFO for the Bank and weighted average for subsidiaries; broken period interest and transaction costs are expensed by the Bank but capitalized by subsidiaries. Disposal of investments is mentioned but not elaborated.

nodes.title: Investments classified as AFS
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting treatment and valuation for investments: AFS debt instruments transfer gains/losses from reserve to P&L; AFS equity transfers to capital reserve. FVTPL/HFT gains/losses recognized in P&L. Subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures: P&L recognition, with profit appropriated to capital reserve after tax/statutory adjustments. HTM: profit recognized in P&L and appropriated to capital reserve; loss recognized in P&L. Short sales of central government securities under HFT are netted, marked to market, losses charged but gains ignored, and settlement gains/losses recognized. Valuation per RBI: HTM at cost with premium/discount amortization; AFS fair valued quarterly with net gains/losses to AFS reserve; FVTPL/HFT fair valued with gains/losses to P&L; subsidiaries/associates/JVs at acquisition cost with amortization and impairment; quoted securities priced by FBIL or other authorized sources; non-INR India-linked bonds via counterparty quotes; discounted instruments at carrying cost.

nodes.title: Investment Accounting Policies and Short Sale Guidelines
key_items: Investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting treatment for investments classified as FVTPL/HFT, subsidiaries/associates/joint ventures, and HTM, detailing recognition of gains/losses in the Profit and Loss Account and appropriations to Capital Reserve and Statutory Reserve after tax adjustments. It also outlines Short Sale transactions in central government dated securities per RBI guidelines, including HFT categorization, netting off, mark-to-market treatment (loss charged, gain ignored), and recognition of gain/loss on settlement.

nodes.title: 5. Valuation:
nodes.summary: The text details RBI guidelines for investment valuation across categories: HTM at cost with premium/discount amortization via SLM (Bank) or EIR (subsidiaries); AFS fair valued quarterly with gains/losses to AFS reserve; FVTPL/HFT fair valued with gains/losses to P&L (HFT daily); subsidiaries/associates/JVs at acquisition cost with impairment assessment. It covers fair value sources (FBIL, exchanges, FIMMDA, counterparty quotes), valuation of discounted instruments, mutual funds, and unquoted investments (yield-based for debt, break-up value for equity, NAV for security receipts/AIFs with haircuts). It also addresses non-performing investments (provisioning, no MTM gains, interest non-recognition) and repo/reverse repo accounting as collateralized borrowings/lendings with interest recognition.

nodes.title: Day 1 gain/ loss on initial recognition
nodes.summary: The text covers day 1 gain/loss recognition on initial measurement of investments at fair value, including presumption of acquisition cost as fair value and situations requiring testing (related parties, outside principal market, duress). It details recognition of day 1 gains/losses (P&L for quoted/observable inputs; immediate loss recognition for Level 3; deferred gains for Level 3 with amortization for debt and liability for unquoted equity). It explains fair value hierarchy (Levels 1-3) and valuation techniques. Transition date accounting per RBI Circular (fair value as revised carrying value, difference adjusted to reserves). For Life Insurance: investment recording at cost on trade date, bonus/rights entitlements recognition, gain/loss on sale computation. Valuation of shareholders' and non-linked policyholders' investments: debt securities at HTM/amortized cost, listed equity at NSE/BSE closing price, unlisted at cost with impairment, InvIT valuation, preference shares at HTM, and impairment recognition/reversal.

nodes.title: Fair Value Hierarchy and Transition Accounting for Life Insurer
key_items: Transition date accounting on 1 st April, 2024
nodes.summary: The page covers day 1 gain deferral for Level 3 investments, including straight-line amortization for debt instruments and liability treatment for unquoted equity until listing or derecognition. It defines fair value and the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1, 2, 3) based on observable versus unobservable inputs, and management's judgment in valuation techniques. Transition date accounting on 1st April 2024 under the RBI Circular dated 12th September 2023 is explained: fair value as of 31st March 2024 becomes revised carrying value, with differences adjusted to Revenue/General Reserve except equity shares in AFS adjusted to AFS Reserve. For the Life Insurance Company, it details initial investment recording at cost on trade date, recognition of bonus and rights entitlements on ex-dates, and computation of gain/loss on transfer or sale using net amortised cost/carrying value on a weighted average basis, with sale consideration net of brokerage and taxes.

nodes.title: Valuation – Shareholders’ Investments and non-linked policy-holders’ investments
nodes.summary: The text details valuation methods for shareholders' and non-linked policyholders' investments: debt securities at HTM/amortized cost; listed equities at NSE/BSE closing prices, unlisted at cost with impairment; InvIT/REIT at NAV if no market quote; mutual funds/AIFs at latest NAV; AT1 bonds at CRISIL yield. It covers impairment recognition/reversal, unrealized gains/losses through fair value change account and P&L, and real estate investment property at cost/revaluation with revaluation reserve. It also addresses hedge accounting for derivatives (cash flow hedges, effectiveness, discontinuation), derivative initial/subsequent recognition at fair value, and NPA classification/provisioning for assets overdue over 90 days per IRDAI regulations.

nodes.title: Valuation – Unit linked Business
nodes.summary: The text details valuation policies for unit-linked insurance business, covering government securities via CRISIL, debt securities using CRISIL bond valuer, accretion of discount on treasury bills, CDs, commercial papers, and triparty repo. Listed shares and ETFs are at fair value (NSE/BSE closing prices), equity shares awaiting listing at historical cost with diminution provisions, and unrealised gains/losses in profit and loss. Mutual funds at latest NAV; unlisted redeemable preference shares as held to maturity at historical cost. Transfers between funds are at book value or market price (lower), with specific rules for debt securities and unit-linked funds. For general insurance, investments at cost including brokerage but excluding pre-acquisition interest; debt securities and non-convertible preference shares as HTM at historical cost adjusted for amortisation/accretion; mutual funds at NAV with unrealised gains/losses in fair value change account and net mark-to-market losses in profit and loss. Gain/loss on sale is difference between sale price and net amortised cost/carrying value on weighted average basis, net of brokerage and taxes. For the bank, RBI guidelines require classification into HFT, AFS, and HTM on purchase date, with subsequent shifting at lower of acquisition cost or carrying value and market value, and depreciation provided. Investments are further classified into six groups. Settlement date accounting is used except for equity shares (trade date). HFT includes investments held for resale within 90 days, reclassified as AFS if unsold after 90 days; HTM for intended-to-maturity investments including subsidiaries, joint ventures, and associates; AFS for the rest.

nodes.title: Investment Valuation Policies for Insurance, Bank, and Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The text outlines investment valuation and accounting policies for financial statements, covering general insurance and banking sectors. For general insurance, it details valuation methods for quoted and unlisted securities, mutual funds, and preference shares, along with transfer rules between funds and recognition of gains/losses. Specific policies for general insurance companies include cost recording, HTM classification for debt securities, NAV-based mutual fund valuation, and gain/loss computation on transfers/sales. For banks, it describes RBI-mandated classification into HFT, AFS, and HTM categories, subsequent shifting rules, and further classification into six groups for balance sheet disclosure, along with settlement date accounting except for equities.

nodes.title: Basis of classification:
nodes.summary: The text outlines the basis of classification for investments into HFT, AFS, and HTM categories, including reclassification rules and treatment of subsidiaries, joint ventures, and associates. It covers acquisition cost determination using weighted average basis, treatment of broken period interest and transaction costs. Disposal of investments details profit/loss recognition for each category. Short sale transactions in Central Government securities are described. Valuation guidelines per RBI are provided for HTM, HFT, and AFS investments, including mark-to-market, amortization, and impairment. It also covers valuation of quoted investments, discounted instruments, mutual funds, and unquoted investments with specific norms for regular and irregular income.

nodes.title: Investment Accounting Policies: Acquisition, Disposal, and Short Sale
nodes.summary: The page covers investment accounting policies: acquisition cost, disposal of investments, and short sale. Acquisition cost is determined on a weighted average basis, with broken period interest treated as revenue and transaction costs recognized in Profit and Loss. Disposal rules vary by classification: HFT and AFS profits/losses go to Profit and Loss; HTM profits are recognized in Profit and Loss and appropriated to Capital Reserve after tax and statutory reserve adjustments, while HTM losses go to Profit and Loss. Short sales of Central Government dated securities follow RBI guidelines, are categorized as HFT, netted off in the Balance Sheet, marked to market with losses charged to Profit and Loss and gains ignored, and settlement gains/losses recognized in Profit and Loss.

nodes.title: Valuation:
nodes.summary: The text outlines RBI guidelines for investment valuation, covering HTM, HFT, and AFS classifications with their respective accounting treatments. It details valuation methods for quoted investments using market prices from stock exchanges, SGL, RBI, or FIMMDA/FBIL; discounted instruments at carrying cost; mutual funds at NAV; and subsidiaries/JVs as HTM with impairment assessment. For unquoted investments, it prescribes methods for bonds/debentures based on interest regularity and credit risk mark-up, equity shares at break-up value, VCF units at NAV or nominal value, and security receipts at lower of NAV or estimated recovery. It also covers AIF provisioning per RBI circulars, non-performing investment identification and provisioning, and accounting for repurchase and reverse repurchase transactions as collateralized borrowings/lendings.

nodes.title: For other entities (other than insurance):
nodes.summary: The text outlines investment accounting for non-insurance entities: classification into long-term and current investments per AS-13 based on holding intent; long-term investments carried at cost with provision for non-temporary diminution; current investments valued at lower of cost (weighted average) or market/fair value, including mutual fund NAV and PTC fair value based on FIMMDA yields marked up for credit risk; stock-in-trade securities valued at lower of cost or market; costs include brokerage and charges; profit/loss on sale recognized on trade date; and NBFC provisions for Alternate Investment Funds per RBI circulars.

nodes.title: G. FOREIGN CURRENCY AND DERIVATIVE TRANSACTIONS
nodes.summary: The text details accounting policies for foreign currency and derivative transactions. For the Bank, it covers translation of monetary assets/liabilities at FEDAI rates, income/expense translation, revaluation of forward/spot contracts, foreign exchange swaps linked to deposits, contingent liabilities, and derivative transactions including fair value recognition, hedge accounting, and off-balance sheet disclosure. It also addresses translation of non-integral overseas operations (IBU and DIFC branch) with exchange differences to Foreign Currency Translation Reserve. For other entities, it covers initial recognition, monetary assets/liabilities at closing rate, exchange differences, forward exchange contracts hedging, and translation of non-integral foreign subsidiaries including disposal treatment. Finally, it details derivative contracts (currency/interest rate/equity/embedded) at fair value, initial margin disclosure, profit/loss on settlement, option premium recognition, and weighted average cost for squaring-up multiple contracts.

nodes.title: H. ADVANCES
key_items: For Bank and NBFC subsidiaries- Provisioning:
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting and provisioning rules for advances. It covers classification into performing and non-performing advances (NPAs) per RBI guidelines, including sub-categories and interest suspense treatment. It details treatment of NPAs acquired from other banks/NBFCs, inter-bank participation with and without risk, and provisioning for NPAs, restructured accounts, standard assets, and frauds. It also includes provisions for country exposure, unhedged foreign currency exposure, COVID-19 moratorium and restructuring provisions, and classification of advances, investments, and derivative overdues. Finally, it covers receivables/sundry debtors valuation and write-off.

nodes.title: I. STRUCTURED LIABILITIES
nodes.summary: The section covers structured liabilities with embedded derivatives separated and debt at amortized cost; policy liabilities for in-force/lapsed policies, discontinued and linked funds; actuarial methods for life insurance including reserves, assumptions, group policies, freelook and reinsurance; reserve for unexpired risk in general insurance; discounted instruments at face value less unexpired discount; acquisition costs expensed; securities lending/borrowing accounting; bullion import and gold borrowing/lending. It details income taxes (current and deferred tax recognition and offset) and segment reporting for banking segments (corporate/wholesale, retail, digital, credit cards, treasury, vehicle financing) under RBI and AS-17 guidelines, including segment definitions, principal activities, transfer pricing by ALCO, and segment revenue/expense/asset/liability treatment. Employee share-based payments are covered: equity-settled ESOPs and PRSUs with accounting under intrinsic value or Black-Scholes, amortization, reversals, and modifications; cash-settled SARs measured at intrinsic or fair value with liability remeasurement. It also includes insurance claims and benefits for life and general insurance subsidiaries, and loss on sale of advances to an ARC.

nodes.title: I. STRUCTURED LIABILITIES (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: structured liabilities with embedded derivatives separated and debt at amortized cost; policy liabilities for in-force/lapsed policies, discontinued and linked funds; actuarial methods for life insurance including reserves, assumptions, group policies, freelook and reinsurance; reserve for unexpired risk in general insurance; discounted instruments at face value less unexpired discount; acquisition costs expensed; securities lending/borrowing accounting; bullion import and gold borrowing/lending; income taxes including current and deferred tax recognition and offset; and segment reporting for banking segments (corporate/wholesale, retail, digital, credit cards, treasury, vehicle financing) under RBI and AS-17 guidelines.

nodes.title: Income Taxes Policy and Segment Reporting Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for income taxes, including current tax measurement in India and overseas, and deferred tax recognition, measurement, review, and offset rules. It also details segment reporting per RBI guidelines and AS-17, defining segments: Corporate/Wholesale Banking, Retail Banking Digital Banking, and Other Retail Banking, which includes lending (commercial vehicle finance, personal loans, home loans, agriculture finance, and other retail exposures meeting Basel criteria) and branch banking (retail borrowings via savings, current, term deposits, branch network, and financial product distribution).

nodes.title: Principal activity
nodes.summary: The text outlines principal activities including other lending, broking, advisory and transactional services, asset management, insurance, securitisation, and services from subsidiary companies. It details brokerage income, interest on delayed payments, distribution of financial products, and advisory services like mergers and acquisitions, equity/debt issue management, and business correspondent services. Asset management covers fund management, investment distribution (Cherry), and life and general insurance until June 17, 2024. A transfer pricing mechanism by ALCO allocates interest costs to segments based on borrowing costs and maturity profiles, disclosed as segment revenue. Segment revenues include external and inter-segment earnings; expenses cover interest, operating expenses, and provisions; results are net of these. Segment assets exclude tax-related assets, and liabilities exclude net worth, minority interest, and employee stock options. The Group operates only in India's domestic segment. Employee share-based payments are mentioned.

nodes.title: Equity-settled:
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's Equity Option Schemes (ESOP) and Performance Linked Restricted Stock Unit Scheme (PRSU) under SEBI regulations, detailing grants of options and restricted stock units to employees. It outlines RBI's clarification that fair value of share-linked instruments granted after March 31, 2021, be expensed. Accounting treatment differs: options granted on or before March 31, 2021, use the intrinsic value method per SEBI and ICAI guidance, while those after use the Black-Scholes model per RBI. Deferred employee compensation is amortized on a straight-line basis over the vesting period, with cumulative expense reflecting vesting progress. Non-vested options due to unmet conditions are reversed, and expired unexercised options transfer balances to General Reserve. Fair market price is the latest closing price preceding the grant date. Modifications to equity-settled awards require minimum expense recognition as if unmodified, with additional expense for value increases or employee benefit.

nodes.title: Cash-settled:
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting for cash-settled stock appreciation rights (SARs) including measurement (intrinsic value for grants on or before March 31, 2021, fair value for later grants), amortization over vesting period, liability remeasurement, and reversal of non-vested SARs. It then details claims and benefits for a Life Insurance subsidiary (death, maturity, surrender, survival, discontinuance, reinsurance recovery, repudiated claims, unit-linked withdrawals) and a General Insurance entity (claims paid net of reinsurance and salvage, loss reserve changes, IBNR/IBNER, survey/legal fees, recognition and provisioning, actuary certification). Finally, it addresses loss on sale of advances to an Asset Reconstruction Company, recognized immediately in profit and loss.

nodes.title: V. SECURITISATION
nodes.summary: The text covers two accounting areas. Securitisation: the Group buys/sells loans via direct assignment or SPVs, often retains servicing, provides credit enhancements (cash collateral or subordination), makes provisions/disclosures under AS-29, and recognizes profit/loss/premium as sale consideration minus book value per RBI guidelines. Leases: as lessee, operating lease payments are expensed on a straight-line basis; as lessor, operating leases (retaining risks/rewards) are in fixed assets with straight-line income and immediate expensing of initial direct costs; finance leases (transferring risks/rewards) are recognized as receivables at net investment, with payments split between finance income and principal repayment.

nodes.title: X. ACCOUNTING FOR PROVISIONS, CONTINGENT LIABILITIES AND CONTINGENT ASSETS
nodes.summary: The section covers accounting policies for provisions, contingent liabilities/assets, including recognition, measurement, credit card reward points actuarial valuation, scheme expenses borne by AMC with brokerage amortization, terrorism/MCET insurance pools, solatium fund contribution, share issue expenses, EPS calculations, asset impairment, cash and cash equivalents, dividend accounting, unclaimed policyholders' funds, and employee benefit contributions. It details gratuity, pension, and compensated absences with reconciliations, actuarial assumptions, and five-year experience adjustments; Long Service Award liability; deposits under lien; securities pledged/encumbered; provisions for reward points, legal, fraud, and contingencies (tax, NPAs, standard assets, COVID-19, forex, investment diminution); COVID-19 provision reversal/holding; tax provisions; contingent liabilities (claims, forex contracts, guarantees, acceptances, legal cases, capital commitments, underwriting, derivatives); and basic/diluted EPS for 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: X. ACCOUNTING FOR PROVISIONS, CONTINGENT LIABILITIES AND CONTINGENT ASSETS (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: provisions, contingent liabilities/assets recognition and measurement; credit card reward points actuarial valuation; scheme expenses borne by AMC including brokerage amortization; participation in Terrorism and MCET insurance pools with retrocession and unearned premium carryforward; solatium fund contribution at 0.10% of motor third-party gross premium; share issue expenses adjusted from securities premium; basic and diluted earnings per share calculations; asset impairment review and loss recognition; cash and cash equivalents components; dividend accounting per AS 4; unclaimed policyholders' amounts managed in segregated fund, NAV-based liability, income accretion, and transfer to SCWF after 120 months; and employee benefit contributions to provident, superannuation, new pension, and DEWS funds with amounts for 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: b. Gratuity
nodes.summary: The text presents detailed disclosures on three employee benefit plans: gratuity, pension, and compensated absences. For gratuity, it outlines the lump-sum benefit terms, reconciliations of defined benefit obligations and plan assets for funded and unfunded portions across two years, expenses recognized, balance sheet liability reconciliation, investment allocation (including LIC-managed funds), actuarial assumptions, five-year experience adjustments, and expected contributions. For pension, it provides similar reconciliations, expense recognition, balance sheet reconciliation, investment details, actuarial assumptions, experience adjustments, and expected contributions. For compensated absences, it states the actuarial liability and assumptions. All monetary amounts are in crore, with comparisons as of March 31, 2025 and 2024.

nodes.title: e. Long Service Award
nodes.summary: The text covers: Long Service Award actuarial liability (₹15.77 crore vs ₹13.56 crore) with discount rate assumptions; deposits under lien (₹9,445.86 crore); securities pledged and encumbered, including Government Securities (face value ₹36,381.85 crore), NSCCL (₹436.92 crore), and CCIL/Stock Exchange (₹323.94 crore); provisions for credit/debit card reward points with movement; legal provisions; fraud and other provisions; breakup of Provisions and Contingencies (total ₹10,902.53 crore vs ₹7,859.02 crore) including tax, NPAs, standard assets, COVID-19, unhedged forex, investment diminution, and other; COVID-19 provision reversal (₹52.83 crore) and holding (₹210.50 crore); provision for taxes (current and deferred); and description of contingent liabilities.

nodes.title: Brief Description
nodes.summary: The text covers contingent liabilities including claims not acknowledged as debts, outstanding forward exchange contracts, guarantees for constituents, acceptances and endorsements, and other contingent items, with a reference to Schedule 12. It includes tax demands, legal cases, and management's view on timing differences. It details foreign exchange contracts, guarantees, documentary credits, bills re-discounted, cash collateral, underwriting commitments, and derivative contracts like swaps and options. It also mentions capital commitments, undrawn investments, and amounts transferred to the DEA Fund. Additionally, it presents earnings per equity share data for years ended March 31, 2025, and 2024, including reconciliations of weighted average shares, basic and diluted EPS, and profit after tax.

nodes.title: 11. EMPLOYEE SHARE BASED PAYMENTS:
nodes.summary: This section covers the Bank's employee share-based payment schemes, including Special Resolutions passed in 2015, 2023, and 2025 to grant options. It details the Kotak Mahindra Equity Option Scheme 2015 (operational for options granted until December 22, 2023), the 2023 scheme, and the Performance Linked Restricted Stock Unit Scheme 2025 (no options granted during the year ended March 31, 2025). It provides data on Plan 2015 and Plan 2023, including grants, vesting periods, exercise periods, vesting conditions, settlement methods, and activity summaries for years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024, with weighted average exercise prices, share prices, and exercise price ranges. It covers Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs) under the 2015 and 2023 schemes, including cash settlement and activity summaries. It explains fair value estimation using Black-Scholes for equity-settled options and remeasurement for cash-settled options, with model inputs and the effect on profit and loss and financial position.

nodes.title: Employee Share Based Payments: Schemes, Resolutions, and Equity Options
nodes.summary: The page covers the Bank's employee share-based payment schemes. Shareholders passed Special Resolutions in 2015, 2023, and 2025 to grant options to eligible employees and subsidiaries. The Kotak Mahindra Equity Option Scheme 2015 and 2023 were formulated; the 2015 scheme is operational only for options granted until December 22, 2023, while the 2023 scheme is in force. The Kotak Mahindra Performance Linked Restricted Stock Unit Scheme 2025 was adopted, but no options were granted under it during the year ended March 31, 2025. Under equity-settled options, the Bank granted options via various schemes, and during the year ended March 31, 2025, Plan 2015 was in operation.

nodes.title: Plan 2023
nodes.summary: The text presents data on employee stock option plans (Plan 2015 and Plan 2023) as of various dates, including details on grants, vesting periods, exercise periods, vesting conditions, and settlement methods. It provides activity summaries for the years ended March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024, showing the number of shares, weighted average exercise prices, granted, forfeited, exercised, expired, and outstanding options. It also includes the weighted average share price at exercise, and a breakdown of exercise prices for outstanding options as of March 31, 2025, by range, with the number of options, weighted average remaining contractual life, and weighted average exercise price. A footnote notes the netting off of unallocated cancelled options.

nodes.title: Outstanding at the end of the year
nodes.summary: The text presents financial statement schedules detailing stock option activity under Plan 2015 and Plan 2023 for the years ended March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. It includes tables showing the number of shares, weighted average exercise prices, grants, forfeitures, exercises, expirations, outstanding and exercisable options, weighted average remaining contractual life, and weighted average fair value. It notes the weighted average share price at exercise date and provides a breakdown of outstanding options by exercise price ranges as of March 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Outstanding at the beginning of the year
nodes.summary: The text presents financial statement schedules detailing stock option activity under Plan 2015 and Plan 2023 for the years ended March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024. It includes tables showing the number of shares, weighted average exercise prices, grants, forfeitures, exercises, expirations, and outstanding and exercisable options, along with weighted average remaining contractual life and fair value of options granted. Additional details cover the weighted average share price at exercise dates and a breakdown of outstanding options by exercise price ranges, number of options, remaining contractual life, and weighted average exercise price for both years.

nodes.title: Stock appreciation rights (SARs)
nodes.summary: The text covers Stock Appreciation Rights (SARs), including a table of weighted average remaining contractual life and exercise prices. It details the 2015 shareholder resolution and Kotak Mahindra SAR Scheme 2015, its replacement by the 2023 Scheme effective December 1, 2023, with the 2015 Scheme handling SARs granted until November 30, 2023. SARs are cash-settled, vest in graded manner, with contractual life of 1.01 to 5.10 years. It summarizes SAR activity for years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024, showing beginning outstanding, granted, settled, forfeited, and ending outstanding numbers, with a note on net-off of 16,050 unallocated cancelled SARs.

nodes.title: Fair value of Employee stock options
nodes.summary: The text details the fair value estimation of employee stock options, distinguishing between equity-settled options (valued at grant date using Black-Scholes) and cash-settled options (remeasured at each balance sheet date). It presents a table of model inputs for years ended March 31, 2025 and 2024, covering both option types, including exercise price, weighted average share price, expected and historical volatility, option life (vesting and exercise period), risk-free interest rate, and expected dividend rate. It explains volatility determination based on historical data and annualized standard deviation. Finally, it outlines the effect of share-based payment plans on the Profit and Loss Account and financial position, including total employee compensation cost, equity-settled compensation cost, liability for outstanding options, deferred compensation cost, and closing liability for cash-settled options.

nodes.summary: This section covers assets taken on lease with operating lease payments and future minimum lease commitments, renewal options, and escalation clauses. It discusses revaluation of investment property by a life insurance subsidiary, reporting market value, historical cost, revaluation gains, and lease payments. It includes forward rate agreements, unhedged forex exposure, and additional information under Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, covering net assets and profit or loss of subsidiaries and associates. Deferred tax liabilities and assets components are presented, along with a fixed assets schedule detailing intangible assets like purchased software, system development expenditure, membership cards, and asset management rights, showing gross block, amortisation, and net block for 2025 and 2024. nodes.title: Deferred Tax Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text presents deferred tax liabilities and assets, detailing components like depreciation, tax deductions, investment fair valuation, and others, with corresponding financial figures for two periods. nodes.title: 22. RELATED PARTY DISCLOSURES:
nodes.summary: This section covers related party disclosures, including identification of related parties such as key management personnel, promoter Mr. Uday S. Kotak, subsidiaries, associates, and enterprises controlled by KMP or their relatives. Transactions are categorized by relationship: associates/others, entities controlled by key managerial personnel (KMP) or individuals with significant influence, KMP/individuals themselves, and their relatives, with amounts in crore and comparative figures in parentheses.

nodes.title: Related Party Transactions: Liabilities, Assets, Commitments, Expenses, Income
nodes.summary: The page presents related party transactions as of/for the year ended 31st March, 2025, organized into four sections. A non-fund/commitments section includes bank guarantees and forward/CIRS outstanding. Section III details expenses comprising salaries (including ESOP cost)/fees, interest paid, and other expenses. Section IV reports income from interest and other sources. Figures are provided for associates/others, with some comparative amounts in parentheses. The page provides a structured overview of all related party transaction categories.

nodes.title: V. Other Transactions

It covers loans repaid, purchases and sales of investments, purchases of fixed assets, and swaps/forwards/options contracts. Figures are given in crore, with current and prior-year comparisons. It also lists material transactions and outstanding balances with related parties such as Zurich Kotak General Insurance Company (India) Limited and Phoenix ARC Private Limited, categorized into liabilities (other liabilities, other payables) and assets (investments).
