nodes.summary: The text presents schedules from a bank's financial statements: advances in India by priority, public, bank, and other sectors; advances outside India from banks and others, including bills and loans; fixed assets covering premises, other fixed assets, and leased assets with gross block, depreciation, and net block for 2025 and 2024; other assets such as accrued interest, advance tax, stationery, derivatives, and others; contingent liabilities including claims, forward contracts, guarantees, acceptances, swaps, options, capital commitments, and unclaimed balances; interest earned from advances, investments, and inter-bank funds; other income from commissions, investment gains, asset sales, exchange profits, dividends, and recoveries; interest expended on deposits, borrowings, and others; operating expenses covering employee costs, rent, printing, advertising, depreciation, director fees, auditor fees, law charges, postage, repairs, insurance, and other expenses; and significant accounting policies detailing the bank's background, basis of preparation, use of estimates, and investment classification and measurement.

nodes.title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Significant Accounting Policies and Basis of Preparation
key_items: A BACKGROUND; C SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.summary: The page covers Schedule 17 of Kotak Mahindra Bank's financial statements, including background, basis of preparation, and significant accounting policies. The background details the bank's history: it was the first NBFC converted to a bank in India, received its banking license in 2003, offers various banking services, and has expanded with an IBU in GIFT City and a branch in DIFC, Dubai. The basis of preparation states that the financial statements comply with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, use accrual and historical cost conventions, and follow Indian GAAP, relevant Companies Act provisions, and RBI guidelines. The use of estimates section explains that management makes prudent estimates and assumptions, with actual results possibly differing, and revisions recognized prospectively.

nodes.title: 1 Investments
nodes.summary: This section outlines the Bank's investment policies, including classification into HTM, AFS, FVTPL, and HFT per RBI guidelines, with detailed criteria for business model assessment and SPPI testing. It covers acquisition cost, disposal treatment, short sales, valuation methods, fair value hierarchy, and day 1 gain/loss recognition. It also details accounting for advances (classification, provisioning, restructuring), fixed assets depreciation, revenue recognition, employee benefits (provident fund, gratuity, pension, compensated absences, share-based payments), foreign currency transactions, derivatives, leases, provisions, impairment, income taxes, dividends, earnings per share, segment reporting, and capital adequacy disclosures including investment portfolio composition.

nodes.title: Investment Classification Policy Under RBI Directions
nodes.summary: The page outlines the Bank's investment policies for the year ended 31st March 2025, covering classification and basis of classification. It references the RBI Master Direction of 12 September 2023, stating that the entire investment portfolio (excluding subsidiaries, joint ventures, and associates) is classified into Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS), and Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVTPL), with Held for Trading (HFT) as a sub-category of FVTPL. Each category is further divided into six groups: Government Securities, Other Approved Securities, Shares, Debentures and Bonds, Investments in Subsidiaries/Joint Ventures, and Other Investments for Balance Sheet disclosure. It also specifies Settlement Date accounting for securities transactions, except Trade Date accounting for equity shares. The basis of classification is the business model for managing investments and their contractual cash flow characteristics.

nodes.title: Business model assessment
nodes.summary: The text details the Bank's assessment of business models for investments, focusing on objectives like earning interest, managing risk, and sales activity, without isolating sales data. It defines 'principal' and 'interest' and outlines criteria for assessing whether contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI), considering reset terms, contingent events, leverage, prepayment, and other features. It explains classification of investments into HTM (held to collect SPPI cash flows), AFS (collect and sell, meeting SPPI, with an irrevocable option for non-trading equity instruments), FVTPL (default), and HFT (trading or short-term gains per RBI Circular). Investments in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures are separately categorized. It covers acquisition cost using FIFO, treatment of broken period interest and transaction costs, and disposal treatment for AFS debt (transfer from AFS Reserve to P&L) and equity instruments (transfer to Capital Reserve).

nodes.title: Investment Classification and Measurement under RBI Guidelines
key_items: Assessment whether contractual cashflows are solely payments of principal and interest
Investments in Subsidiaries, Associates and Joint Ventures
nodes.summary: The page covers the assessment of whether contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI), including consideration of reset terms, contingent events, leverage, prepayment, extension, non-recourse arrangements, and time value modifications. It details classification criteria for investments at held-to-maturity (HTM), available-for-sale (AFS), fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL), and held-for-trading (HFT). It addresses investments in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures as a separate category. Finally, it explains acquisition cost determination on a FIFO basis, treatment of broken period interest as an expense, and recognition of transaction costs in profit and loss.

nodes.title: Disposal of investments: Investments classified as AFS
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting treatment for disposal of investments across categories: AFS (debt and equity), FVTPL/HFT, subsidiaries/associates/JVs, and HTM, detailing gain/loss recognition and reserve appropriations. It covers short sale transactions under RBI guidelines, including categorization, netting, mark-to-market, and gain/loss recognition. Valuation rules per RBI guidelines are specified: HTM at cost with SLM amortization; AFS quarterly fair value with net gains/losses to AFS reserve; FVTPL/HFT fair value with gains/losses to P&L (HFT daily, others quarterly); subsidiaries/associates/JVs at cost with impairment assessment; fair value sources (FBIL, exchanges, FIMMDA, counterparty quotes); discounted instruments at carrying cost; mutual funds at latest NAV; and unquoted instruments per RBI norms.

nodes.title: Accounting Treatment for Various Investment Categories and Short Sales
key_items: Investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures
nodes.summary: This page covers accounting treatment for investments classified as FVTPL/HFT, subsidiaries/associates/JVs, and HTM, plus short sales. For FVTPL/HFT, gains/losses on sale go to Profit and Loss. For subsidiaries/associates/JVs, profit/loss on sale is recognized in Profit and Loss, with profit appropriated to Capital Reserve after tax and statutory reserve transfer. For HTM, profit on sale/redemption goes to Profit and Loss and appropriated to Capital Reserve after adjustments; losses are charged to Profit and Loss. Short sales of Central Government dated securities follow RBI guidelines, categorized under HFT, netted off in the Balance Sheet, marked to market with losses charged to Profit and Loss and gains ignored; settlement gains/losses are recognized in Profit and Loss.

nodes.title: Valuation:
nodes.summary: The text outlines RBI-compliant valuation guidelines for various investments: HTM at cost with straight-line amortization; AFS fair-valued quarterly with gains/losses to reserves; FVTPL/HFT fair-valued with gains/losses to P&L (daily for HFT, quarterly for others); subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures at cost with impairment assessment. It specifies fair value sources (FBIL, exchanges, FIMMDA), treatment of non-INR bonds, discounted instruments at carrying cost, mutual funds at NAV, and valuation norms for unquoted instruments, equity shares, security receipts, and AIFs. It covers NPIs (depreciation per RBI, no MTM gains, interest not recognized until received, security receipts over 8 years as NPI) and repo/reverse repo accounting as collateralized borrowings/lendings with interest recognition.

nodes.title: Day 1 gain/ loss on initial recognition
nodes.summary: The text covers day 1 gain/loss on initial recognition of investments, stating all investments are measured at fair value initially, with acquisition cost presumed as fair value unless facts suggest otherwise. It lists situations where this presumption is tested: related party transactions, transactions outside the principal market, and duress transactions. It notes no day 1 gain/loss is expected for investments executed through trading platforms or recognized stock exchanges, but day 1 gain/loss is tested for transactions outside the principal market or with related parties. For quoted securities or fair value based on market observable inputs, any day 1 gain/loss is recognized in Profit and Loss. For Level 3 investments, day 1 losses are recognized immediately, while day 1 gains are deferred: amortized straight-line to maturity for debt instruments, or set aside as a liability until listing or derecognition for unquoted equity instruments.

nodes.title: Fair Value Hierarchy:
nodes.summary: The text defines fair value and outlines a three-level hierarchy (Level 1, 2, 3) based on observable inputs, noting management judgment in valuation techniques. It covers transition date accounting per RBI Circular dated September 12, 2023, adjusting differences between fair value and carrying value in Revenue/General Reserve or AFS Reserve for equity shares. Investment policies for the year ended March 31, 2024, include classification into HFT, AFS, and HTM categories, further grouped into six asset types, with settlement date accounting except for equity shares. It details basis of classification (HFT resale within 90 days, HTM held to maturity, AFS residual), acquisition cost (weighted average, broken period interest as revenue, transaction costs in P&L), disposal treatment for HFT/AFS and HTM (with capital reserve appropriation), and short sale transactions in government securities categorized as HFT, netted off, marked to market with loss charged and gain ignored.

nodes.title: Investment Classification and Fair Value Accounting Policies
key_items: Transition date accounting as on 1 st April, 2024
Policies applicable for the year ended 31 st March, 2024:
nodes.summary: The page covers fair value hierarchy levels (1, 2, 3) and transition date accounting as on 1st April 2024, where fair value as on 31st March 2024 becomes revised carrying value, with differences adjusted to Revenue/General Reserve or AFS Reserve. It details policies for the year ended 31st March 2024: classification into HFT, AFS, HTM and six groups, with shifting rules; basis of classification (HFT held for resale within 90 days, HTM held to maturity, AFS residual); acquisition cost determined on weighted average basis, broken period interest as revenue, and transaction costs in Profit and Loss; and disposal treatment for HFT/AFS (profit/loss in P&L) and HTM (profit appropriated to Capital Reserve after adjustments, loss in P&L).

nodes.title: Short Sale:
nodes.summary:
Short Sale:
The Bank undertakes short sale transactions in Central Government dated securities in accordance with RBI guidelines. The short position is categorised under HFT category and netted off from Investments in the Balance Sheet. The short position is marked to market and loss, if any, is charged to the Profit and Loss Account while gain, if any, is ignored. Gain or loss on settlement of the short position is recognised in the Profit and Loss Account.226

nodes.title: Valuation:
nodes.summary: The text details investment valuation per RBI guidelines, covering HTM, HFT, and AFS classifications, including amortization, mark-to-market, and provisioning for diminution. It specifies valuation methods for quoted and unquoted instruments, mutual funds, subsidiaries, venture capital funds, security receipts, and alternative investment funds. It also addresses non-performing investments, repurchase transactions, and advances classification into performing and non-performing, including provisioning norms, restructuring, and general provisions. Finally, it covers loss on sale of advances to Asset Reconstruction Companies.

nodes.title: Advances Classification and Inter-Bank Participation Guidelines
nodes.summary: The page details RBI-based classification of advances into performing and non-performing (NPAs), including sub-standard, doubtful, and loss assets. It explains netting adjustments for rediscounted bills, inter-bank participation with risk, specific provisions, interest in suspense, ECGC and ECLGS claims, and restructured asset provisions. Interest on NPAs goes to a suspense account until collected. Advances acquired from other banks/NBFCs are treated as advances, with overdue classification based on cash flow estimates exceeding 90 days. It also covers inter-bank participation with and without risk, specifying whether amounts are reduced from advances, classified under advances, or shown as borrowings depending on the Bank’s role.

nodes.title: Provisioning:
nodes.summary: The text covers provisioning and accounting policies: classification of advances, investments, and derivatives into performing/non-performing per RBI guidelines; NPA provisioning including accelerated specific provisioning charged to P&L, with recoveries recognized; restructured accounts definition, conditions, and fair value provision; COVID-19 restructuring provisions held higher than RBI requirements; general provisions on standard assets including derivatives, gold, overseas stepdown subsidiaries, stressed sectors, frauds, and moratorium accounts; country exposure provisions based on ECGC risk categories; unhedged foreign currency exposure provisions; loss on sale of advances to ARC recognized immediately; securitisation accounting including credit enhancements and profit/loss recognition per RBI guidelines; fixed assets stated at cost less depreciation/amortization and impairment, with capitalization and disposal policies, and depreciation on straight-line method over useful lives at rates equal to or higher than Companies Act Schedule II.

nodes.title: Asset Type
nodes.summary: The text covers asset types and their useful lives for depreciation, including leasehold land and improvements, office equipment, computers, furniture, vehicles, ATMs, and software, with special rules for used assets and low-cost items. It details accounting for cash and cash equivalents, bullion transactions (import, sale, borrowing, lending), and revenue recognition policies for interest income (various methods), service charges, fees, commissions, dividends, securitisation gains/losses, NPAs, and Priority Sector Lending Certificates. Finally, it outlines employee benefit plans: Provident Fund, Superannuation Fund, New Pension Scheme, and DIFC Employee Workplace Savings Scheme, noting contribution limits and expense recognition.

nodes.title: Financial Statements Schedules: Revenue Recognition and Employee Benefits
nodes.summary: The page details revenue recognition policies, including accrual-based interest income using methods like internal rate of return and straight-line for various instruments, recognition of fees, commissions, dividends, and securitization gains/losses, treatment of non-performing assets, and income from priority sector lending certificates. It also covers employee benefits under defined contribution plans: Provident Fund contributions to government or bank funds with no further obligation; Superannuation Fund contributions up to ₹0.01 crore per employee per annum to a trustee-administered fund managed by life insurers; and New Pension Scheme contributions up to 10% of salary to a PFRDA-appointed pension fund manager, all expensed when service is rendered.

nodes.title: DIFC Employee Workplace Savings Scheme (DEWS)
nodes.summary: The text details various employee benefit plans: DIFC DEWS contributions (8.33% of salary) expensed as incurred; Defined Benefit Gratuity actuarially determined via Projected Unit Credit Method with trustee-managed funds; Pension Scheme for erstwhile ING Vysya employees (10% of basic salary, actuarial true-up, no provident fund eligibility); Compensated Absences accrued actuarially; Other Employee Benefits including service awards and short-term benefits like performance incentives; and Equity-settled share-based payments covering ESOS and PRSU schemes under SEBI regulations, with accounting policy change from intrinsic to fair value method for grants after March 31, 2021 per RBI guidance. Actuarial gains/losses are recognized immediately in Profit and Loss.

nodes.title: Employee Benefit Plans and Obligations
key_items: Compensated Absences – Other Long-Term Employee Benefits
nodes.summary: The page details four employee benefit areas. Defined Benefit Plan Gratuity covers actuarially determined gratuity liability via Projected Unit Credit Method with contributions to trustee-administered funds managed by life insurers. Pension Scheme addresses contributions for erstwhile ING Vysya Bank employees under IBA structure, actuarial true-ups, fund administration, ineligibility for provident fund, recognition of plan assets, and immediate recognition of actuarial gains/losses. Compensated Absences – Other Long-Term Employee Benefits accrues liability based on actuarial valuation with assumptions and recognizes gains/losses immediately. Other Employee Benefits include service awards measured actuarially and short-term benefits like performance incentives recognized when service is rendered.

nodes.title: Employee share based payments Equity-settled scheme:
nodes.summary: The text details employee share-based payments, covering equity-settled schemes (ESOS and PRSU) with accounting policy change from intrinsic to fair value for grants after March 31, 2021, per RBI guidelines; treatment of lapsed/expired options, modifications, and subsidiary cost recovery. Cash-settled SARs similarly transition to fair value. Foreign currency transactions section covers translation of monetary items, income/expenses, forward/spot contracts, swaps, contingent liabilities, and non-integral overseas operations. Derivative transactions section covers recognition at fair value, hedge accounting, option premiums, and mark-to-market.

nodes.title: Share-Based Payments and Foreign Currency Transaction Accounting
nodes.summary: The page outlines accounting for share-based payments, including equity-settled options, modifications, subsidiary recoveries, and cash-settled stock appreciation rights (SARs) with vesting, measurement, and liability remeasurement rules. It also covers foreign currency transactions: translation of monetary assets/liabilities at FEDAI rates, income/expenditure at transaction or average rates, revaluation of forward/spot contracts, swap premium amortization, contingent liabilities at year-end rates, and translation of non-integral overseas operations with exchange differences to Foreign Currency Translation Reserve.

nodes.title: 11 Derivative transactions
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: derivative transactions (recognition at fair value, hedge accounting, option premiums); lease accounting (operating leases expensed straight-line, initial direct costs expensed); provisions, contingent liabilities and assets (recognition criteria, measurement, disclosure); impairment (review and loss provision); income taxes (current and deferred tax, recognition criteria, measurement, offsetting); dividend accounting (no provision for post-balance sheet dividends); and earnings per share (basic EPS calculation and adjustments).

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Leases, Provisions, Impairment, Taxes, Dividends
key_items: 13 Accounting for provisions, contingent liabilities and contingent assets
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies: operating leases are expensed straight-line with initial direct costs expensed immediately; provisions are recognized for probable outflows, reviewed at each balance sheet date, and contingent liabilities disclosed when losses are possible but not estimable, while contingent assets are not recognized or disclosed; impairment losses are provided when asset carrying amounts exceed recoverable amounts; income tax expense includes current and deferred tax, with deferred tax assets recognized based on reasonable or virtual certainty of future taxable income, reassessed at each reporting date, and offset under legal rights; and dividends proposed after the balance sheet date are not provided for but appropriated from the next year's amount.

nodes.title: 17 Earnings per share
nodes.summary: The text covers earnings per share (basic and diluted calculations, including adjustments for bonus issues, rights issues, and share splits), share issue expenses adjusted against securities premium, credit card reward points liability estimated via actuarial valuation, and segment reporting. Segment reporting details the segregation of the Bank’s business into Treasury, BMU and Corporate Centre; Corporate/Wholesale Banking; Retail Banking (including Digital Banking, Other Retail Banking with lending, branch banking, and credit cards); and Other Banking business. It explains segment revenues, expenses, results, assets, and liabilities, including transfer pricing by ALCO, and notes that operations are primarily domestic, so only the domestic segment is reported.

nodes.title: Financial Statements Schedules: Share Expenses, Credit Cards, Segment Reporting
nodes.summary: The page covers diluted earnings per share adjustments for dilutive potential equity shares, share issue expenses adjusted from Securities Premium Account under Section 52, and credit card reward points liability estimated via actuarial valuation. It also details segment reporting per RBI guidelines and AS-17, listing segments: Treasury, BMU and Corporate Centre; Corporate/Wholesale Banking; Retail Banking; Digital Banking; Other Retail Banking. Principal activities described include money market, forex, derivatives, investments, government securities primary dealership, asset liability management, support functions, wholesale borrowings/lendings, digital banking products, and other retail banking subdivided into lending (commercial vehicle finance, personal loans, home loans, agriculture finance, other retail exposures), branch banking (retail borrowings, branch network, financial product distribution), and credit cards (receivables/loans).

nodes.title: Other Banking business
nodes.summary: The text covers segment reporting and capital adequacy disclosures. It details a transfer pricing mechanism by ALCO for interest cost allocation, defines segment revenues, expenses, results, assets, and liabilities, and notes the Bank operates only domestically. It presents Basel III capital adequacy ratios for March 31, 2025 and 2024, including CET1, Tier I, Tier II, total capital, RWAs, various ratios, leverage ratio, government shareholding, and capital raised. Additionally, it provides the composition of the investment portfolio as of both dates, categorized by investments in India and outside, and by HTM, AFS, and HFT, including gross and net values, provisions for non-performing investments, and unrealized gains/losses, along with details on pledged securities.

nodes.title: 3. MOVEMENT OF PROVISIONS FOR DEPRECIATION AND INVESTMENT FLUCTUATION RESERVE:
nodes.summary: The text presents financial disclosures in two main sections. Section 3 details the movement of provisions for depreciation on investments, showing opening balance, additions, write-backs/transfers, and closing balance (with a note on NPI), and the movement of Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR), including opening balance, transfers, drawdown, closing balance, and IFR as a percentage of investments in AFS and HFT/Current Category, for the years ended 31st March 2025 and 2024. Section 4 provides details of repo/reverse repo deals (excluding LAF and MSF) for the same years, listing minimum, maximum, daily average, and outstanding balances as of year-end for securities sold under repos (government securities, corporate debt securities, other securities) and securities purchased under reverse repos, with both Market Value (MV) and Face Value (FV) reported.

The Operations section describes Consumer Banking's customer segments, products, and digital focus; reorganization into Product, Distribution, and Proposition segments; persona-driven branch design; new Kotak Mobile Banking App; Voice platform bridging digital and physical channels; curated propositions like Kotak Solitaire; customer 360 engagement; and branch decongestion and frontline digitization initiatives including TAS, reduced batch processing, and an AI-powered bot.

nodes.summary: The page covers credit ratings, deposits, removal of supervisory restrictions, and operations. Deposit disclosures under Rule 8(5)(v) and (vi) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, read with Sections 73 and 74 of the Act, are not applicable as the entity is a banking company. Regarding removal of supervisory restrictions, an RBI order dated 24 April 2024 had directed the Bank to cease onboarding new customers via online and mobile banking and issuing fresh credit cards due to IT examination deficiencies for 2022 and 2023. RBI's letter dated 12 February 2025 lifted these restrictions after remedial measures and compliance submissions, including an external auditor's report. Operations are mentioned but no details are provided.

nodes.summary: The Consumer Banking section covers its wide customer base and product range, a customer-centric digital strategy, and reorganization into Product, Distribution, and Proposition segments. Distribution uses branch, digital, and voice channels; branches are persona-driven, a new mobile app launched, and voice integrates support. Product strategy shifted to differentiated, segment-relevant propositions like Kotak Solitaire. Customer engagement uses a 360 approach with data analytics for risk underwriting. Branch service focuses on decongestion and frontline digitization. Results include 11% deposit growth (18% ActivMoney), 17% consumer assets growth, secured business up 19%, unsecured loans up 24%, and a ₹3,330 crore personal loan acquisition. Kotak811 highlights include restarted acquisition, enhanced app, and hybrid support. Customer service improved with Salesforce and a 28% reduction in complaints.

nodes.title: COMMERCIAL BANKING
nodes.summary: The Commercial Banking division serves CV, CE, TFE, Agri-value-chain SMEs, and Microcredit, mainly in semi-urban/rural priority sectors, advancing financial inclusion. CV industry declined ~1% while the Bank grew 2% in units; CE grew 2%; disbursements rose 6% YoY, gaining market share. Slow growth was due to election code, heat wave, and lower government spending, causing collection deterioration, but risk analytics and credit policy improved Q4 FY25. Tractor industry grew ~7%; the Bank matched growth, maintained leadership, with over 90% PSL loans. Kharif/Rabi output was stable; ABG followed a risk-calibrated NTB strategy. Microcredit faced delinquency from over-leveraging, weak monsoons, heat wave, and floods; the Bank was cautious, credit costs rose, and collections improved in Q4 post-SRO guardrails. Gold loans grew 56% industry-wide; the Bank offers them from 480+ branches (~25% of network). PSL guidelines require 40% of ANBC; average PSL was ₹139,713.24 crore (45.09% of ANBC) vs. 44.06% prior year.

nodes.title: WHOLESALE BANKING
nodes.summary: The text details the Bank's Wholesale Banking business, covering its diverse corporate client segments and comprehensive product suite. It highlights strategic growth in SME and Mid-Market segments, restructuring for emerging corporates, and increased share in short-term and working capital loans, trade finance, and transaction banking. It notes challenges like muted credit demand and tight liquidity, mitigated by strategic initiatives. The Bank leverages Centres-of-Excellence in structured lending, infrastructure, real estate, financial sponsors, and custody. It excelled in capital markets, handling 19 mainboard IPOs and strong custody flows. Digital investments include the Kotak fyn platform with growth metrics, omni-channel trade approvals, process simplification, automation, DIY journeys, and the Sampark Setu merchant platform. International Banking Units in GIFT City and DIFC are described, including regulatory details and services like overseas loans, ECB, forex, derivatives, and global investments. Asset Reconstruction covers distressed asset investments, resolution through judicial forums, and FY 2024-25 investments. Treasury includes Balance Sheet Management, Proprietary Trading, and Customer Transactions across forex, derivatives, and bullion.

nodes.title: TECHNOLOGY AND DIGITISATION

The Bank built an in-house engineering team to reduce vendor reliance and develop unified platforms. Key initiatives include upgrading the Core Banking Solution with horizontal and vertical layers, strengthening IT governance and cybersecurity; creating unified interoperable platforms for seamless integration; and leveraging data analytics with AI/ML for predictive insights and automation. It also highlights building Kotak AI, a proprietary Generative AI platform. The transformation enabled fast, intuitive, secure digital apps for diverse segments: a new Kotak Bank App for affluent, non-resident, and self-employed customers; Kotak811 for core India; and Sampark Setu for merchants. The year marked a pivotal step in modernizing infrastructure and enhancing customer experience.

nodes.summary:
TRADING OF SHARES TO BE IN COMPULSORILY DEMATERIALISED FORM
The equity shares of the Bank are traded only in dematerialised form. Transfer of shares held in physical form cannot be processed.
Pursuant to the SEBI Listing Regulations, the Bank shall (i) effect issuance of certificates in dematerialised form only, for any requests received for sub-division, split, consolidation, renewal, exchanges, endorsements or issuance of duplicate certificates; and (ii) execute requests for transmission and transposition of securities, held in physical or dematerialised form, in dematerialised form only. Investors holding shares in physical form are advised to dematerialize their existing holdings.

nodes.summary:
Customer Centricity at the Core
This year, the focus continues to be on customer centricity and the Bank has built propositions around this principle by leveraging digital capabilities. In FY 2024-25, the Bank has undertaken changes across its Distribution, Product and Proposition frameworks—designed to deliver unique, meaningful and relevant propositions.

nodes.title: Strategically organised the distribution architecture to align with customer personas
nodes.summary: The text details the Bank's strategic distribution architecture realigned across physical, digital, and voice channels to serve defined customer personas. It covers branch design tailored to personas, digital app enhancements including the new Kotak Mobile Banking App, and the voice platform bridging channels. It explains the shift to differentiated, segment-relevant product propositions and the launch of Kotak Solitaire, an invite-only affluent banking proposition with exclusive features. It also covers frontline empowerment through branch decongestion and digitization, and reports an 11% deposit growth with 18% growth in ActivMoney, along with branch and ATM numbers as of March 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Customer-Centric Propositions, Kotak Solitaire, and Frontline Service Excellence
key_items: Curated propositions through the customer lens
Driving service excellence through frontline empowerment
nodes.summary: The Bank shifted from a uniform to a differentiated, segment-relevant product strategy balancing cost efficiency and customer value. It curates bespoke propositions for key financial use cases, uses personas and customer 360 data analytics for engagement and risk underwriting. Kotak Solitaire, an invite-only affluent banking proposition, harnesses the Kotak Group product suite with a dedicated relationship manager, wealth management, 3-in-1 banking/trading/demat, pricing benefits, pre-approved loans, an exclusive credit card with premium travel perks, and entrepreneur-focused cash flow and lending solutions. To drive service excellence, the Bank focuses on branch decongestion via digital and voice channels, and frontline digitisation initiatives including faster transaction processing, reduced batch processing, and an AI-powered bot.

nodes.title: Strengthening the liabilities franchise
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's liability franchise strengthening with 11% deposit growth, driven by 18% ActivMoney growth and persona-based approach optimizing deposit mix. It details branch and ATM network expansion to 2,148 branches and 3,295 ATMs/recyclers, including DIFC and GIFT City branches. It discusses consumer assets growth: 17% overall, secured business (Home Loans, LAP, Working Capital) at 19%, unsecured loans (excluding credit cards) at 24%, and acquisition of a ₹3,330 crore personal loan portfolio from Standard Chartered Bank India. It highlights mortgage and LAP focus, business banking strengthening with offerings like Biz-Buddy, Integrated Solutions, and digital tools (WhatsApp Banking, AI chatbot), and technology-led engagement initiatives including digital journeys, data analytics, and Customer 360 approach.

nodes.title: Consumer Assets Growth, Mortgage Focus, and Business Banking Advances
key_items: Building Momentum on Assets while managing risk
nodes.summary: The page covers building momentum on assets while managing risk, detailing consumer assets growth of 17% year-on-year despite RBI credit card restrictions, including a ₹3,330 crore personal loan portfolio acquisition. It highlights secured business growth of 19% in home loans, LAP, and working capital, and unsecured loans growth of 24%. Consumer banking advances are shown from Mar-21 to Mar-25. The mortgage business's strategic focus, LAP market steadiness, and new loan origination system benefits are discussed. Business banking strengthening, secured SME portfolio performance, and new offerings like Biz-Buddy AI recommendation engine, integrated payment solutions, WhatsApp Banking, and AI-enabled chatbot for merchant engagement are also covered.

nodes.title: Technology-led engagement
nodes.summary: The text covers technology-led engagement initiatives including seamless digital journeys, integrated data analytics for risk underwriting and customer profiling, and a refreshed Customer 360 approach to deepen relationships with products like Home Loans and LAP. It highlights Kotak811's FY 2024-25 integration of advanced technologies to enhance customer experience, restart acquisition with AI/ML, enhance the app with 100+ features, optimize physical interactions via hybrid platforms, and focus on better-quality customers through 811Super. It also notes strengthened customer service via Salesforce and Kaizen, resulting in a 28% YoY reduction in net complaints. Commercial Banking's focus on CV, CE, Tractor, Agri SMEs and Microcredit, its five-year advances trend, and Commercial Vehicle segment performance are also summarized.

nodes.title: Kotak811, Strategic Focus, Customer Service, and Commercial Banking Advances
nodes.summary: The page covers Kotak811's FY 2024-25 integration of AI/ML for secure onboarding, revamped app with 100+ features and digital journeys, and hybrid platforms enabling sales officers to offer multiple services. Strategic focus includes acquiring higher-quality customers, 811Super with 5% cashback, and early engagement driving product penetration. Customer service strengthened via Salesforce automation and Kaizen principles, reducing net complaints by 28% YoY. Commercial Banking serves CV, CE, Tractor, Agri-SME, and Microcredit segments, largely semi-urban/rural priority sector, supporting financial inclusion. Commercial advances grew from ₹53,529 crore in Mar-21 to ₹95,579 crore in Mar-25.

nodes.title: Commercial Vehicle
nodes.summary: The text reviews FY 2024-25 performance across business segments. Commercial Vehicle industry declined 1% YoY; the Bank grew 2%, with goods down 3% and passenger up 16%, while collection faced challenges from lower load availability and excess supply. Construction Equipment industry grew 2%, Bank disbursements up 6%, with collection deterioration but Q4 improvement. Tractor industry grew 7%, Bank maintained leadership, with 90% PSL-eligible loans. Agri Business had stable portfolio quality with risk-calibrated growth. Microcredit faced delinquency rise due to over-leveraging and weather impacts, with cautious disbursements and Q4 collection improvement. Gold Loan industry grew 56%, Bank offers it from 480+ branches. Wholesale Banking details units, offerings, and focus on quality customers. Industry credit demand was mixed: SME and certain services grew faster, but private capex, urban/rural consumption, and government capex remained muted.

nodes.title: Banking Sector Performance: Equipment, Agri, Microcredit, Gold Loan, Wholesale
nodes.summary: The page reviews FY 2024-25 performance across banking segments. Construction Equipment grew 2% YoY, with Bank disbursements up 6% despite election, weather, and liquidity challenges; collections improved in Q4. Tractor industry grew 7%, Bank maintained leadership with 90% PSL-eligible loans. Agri Business remained stable with risk-calibrated growth. Microcredit faced delinquency issues from over-leveraging and weather events; cautious disbursements and guardrails improved Q4 collections. Gold Loan industry grew 56%, with Bank offering loans from 480+ branches. Wholesale Banking serves diverse clients with customized solutions, focusing on quality customer acquisition and cross-selling. The text also covers load availability and collection environment challenges.

nodes.title: Industry
nodes.summary: The text discusses mixed credit demand in FY 2024-25, with faster SME growth but muted private capex and urban consumption. Tight liquidity and buoyant capital markets constrained bank lending spreads, prompting the Wholesale Bank to reinvent its business model by focusing on short-term loans, trade and supply chain, digital initiatives, and cross-selling to boost liability and fee incomes. It emphasizes granular growth in SME and mid-market segments through customer acquisition strategies, digital platforms, and data analytics, while maintaining healthy asset quality. The Bank developed Centres of Excellence for structured lending, infrastructure, real estate, and financial sponsors. Infrastructure lending focuses on high-rated borrowers, diversification, and tailored solutions, with notable deals in roads, renewables, and digital infrastructure. The Bank won the 'Best Bank for Large Corporates in India' award.

nodes.title: Wholesale Bank Strategy: Business Model, Granular Growth, and Centers of Excellence
nodes.summary: The text discusses the Wholesale Bank's response to tight liquidity, elevated cost of funds, and competitive pressures. It covers reinventing the business model by reducing asset income dependence, increasing short-term loans, strengthening trade and supply chain, and digital initiatives to boost liability and fee incomes, resulting in profitability and an award. It highlights granular growth through higher SME and mid-market growth, customer acquisition, retention strategies, digital platforms, data analytics, cross-selling, and healthy asset quality. Finally, it describes Centers of Excellence in structured lending, infrastructure financing, real estate financing, and financial sponsors banking, leveraging expertise for profitability.

nodes.title: Infrastructure Lending
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's wholesale banking segments: infrastructure lending (focus on high-rated groups, diversified sectors, private equity/pension-backed platforms, InvITs, tailored solutions by project stage, debt capital market access, and deals in roads, renewables, digital infrastructure); real estate lending (muted growth due to repayments, focus on profitability via rebalancing, optimistic outlook); financial sponsors (dedicated coverage of large funds, market share in flows and structured solutions, robust growth); multinational companies (full suite of services, 'Catch them young' philosophy, ING partnership, corridor strategy, Korea and Japan desks, Hyundai IPO); financial institutions (steady asset quality, selective growth, priority sector on-lending to NBFCs, calibrated unsecured lending); overseas book (GIFT City branch, enhanced technology, trade and loan product growth, relationship-backed transactions); a five-year trend of wholesale banking advances; and syndication and debt capital markets (highest-ever DCM fees, record volumes, large deals across bonds, real estate, and infrastructure).

nodes.title: Wholesale Banking Segments Performance and Advances
nodes.summary: The page reviews real estate lending with muted growth, portfolio rebalancing, and a strong pipeline; financial sponsors coverage for funds and investee companies with robust income growth; multinational companies focusing on India as a manufacturing hub, digital services, ING partnership, corridor desks, and a major IPO; financial institutions with steady asset quality and selective lending to NBFCs; and the overseas book strengthened via GIFT City with enhanced technology and trade loan growth. It also presents the five-year trend of wholesale banking advances, including corporate banking and SME.

nodes.title: Syndication and Debt Capital Markets
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's Syndication and Debt Capital Markets achievements, including record DCM fees from diverse deals in bonds, real estate, infrastructure, and various sectors, and assisting corporates in bond market access. It highlights focus on Transaction Banking and non-asset income streams like Forex and Cash Management to boost Returns on Equity. Trade financing efforts include new products, digitization, paperless imports, GIFT City branch launch, fyn platform expansion with Bank Guarantees, a dedicated help desk, and process improvements. Supply Chain Finance uses a three-pronged approach with digital journeys and fintech collaborations. Cash Management Services emphasize digital-first solutions, 36% transaction value growth, product innovations, risk management, enhanced e-collections, tax payment growth, and leadership in capital markets with 19 mainboard IPOs.

nodes.title: Transaction Banking, Trade Financing, and Supply Chain Finance Growth
key_items: Focus on Transaction Banking and Non-Asset Income Streams
nodes.summary: The page covers the Bank's transaction banking and non-asset income streams, highlighting growth in non-credit income like Forex, Cash Management, and Transaction Banking products to boost Returns on Equity. It details trade financing expansion through new products, paperless imports, GIFT City branch capabilities, fyn platform enhancements including Bank Guarantees, a dedicated help desk that trained over 1,500 clients, and improved turnaround times via feedback analysis. Supply Chain Finance focus includes granular business, structured trade deals, digital SCF journeys, and fintech collaborations. Both Trade and Supply Chain books saw strong growth, increasing customer flows, liability, and fee incomes. The Bank also facilitated 418 transactions across infrastructure and other sectors and helped corporate customers access bond markets competitively.

nodes.title: Transaction Banking and Cash Management Services
nodes.summary: The Bank advanced its digital-first Cash Management Services (CMS) strategy, focusing on customized solutions, current account growth, and cross-selling. Transaction value rose 36% YoY. Innovations included enterprise payment resiliency, API-based processing, risk management investments, and an enhanced CMS stack for mutual funds, payment aggregators, and BFSI. A new e-collections platform offered near-real-time posting. Tax payments grew 2x in value. The Bank strengthened capital markets, handling 19 mainboard IPOs worth over ₹84,000 crore. Customer experience improved with an 80% reduction in onboarding TAT. The Bank received multiple accolades. Rising funding costs renewed focus on liabilities, core current accounts, term deposits, and non-risk income.

nodes.title: Custodial Services
nodes.summary:
Custodial Services
Offshore Custody flows remained strong for larger part of the year on the back of strong capital markets. Market volatility has impacted the flows towards the end of the year. While foreign institutional investors were cautious, domestic institutions saw increased activity. During the year, the Bank continued to deepen its market penetration and successfully on-boarded new clients across both domestic and offshore custody businesses, positioning itself well for future growth. Average custody balances grew strongly during the year.
In FY 2024-25, we secured a license in GIFT City to provide Global Custody Services, expanding our capability to provide custodial services for assets held internationally. This initiative enables us to support both our domestic and offshore clients as they invest in a broader range of foreign asset classes, reinforcing our commitment to offering comprehensive, cross-border solutions.

nodes.title: Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text covers Risk Management, highlighting diversified portfolio, internal credit ratings, risk-adjusted pricing, and focus on risk-return balance to maintain low credit costs and optimize risk-weighted assets. Treasury discusses global and Indian market trends, RBI rate cuts, INR depreciation, and desks' strategies. Private Banking serves ultra-HNI clients, added 2,692 families, and won awards. Asset Reconstruction invests in stressed assets, expects opportunities. GIFT City branch offers trade loans, custody, and digital services. DIFC branch provides global investment products. Subsidiary KMPL reports financials: PBT ₹1,356.86 crore, NPA ratios, and technology initiatives for auto financing.

nodes.title: Kotak Mahindra Prime Limited Subsidiary Highlights 2024-25
nodes.summary: Kotak Mahindra Prime Limited (KMPL) provides retail financing for cars, MUVs, two-wheelers, dealer working capital and infrastructure loans, and LAP. Financial highlights show FY 2024-25 net interest income ₹2,133.42 crore, other income ₹686.35 crore, total income ₹2,819.77 crore, operating expenses ₹1,123.38 crore, provisions ₹339.53 crore, PBT ₹1,356.86 crore, and PAT ₹1,015.47 crore, with comparative FY 2023-24 figures. Net customer assets were ₹40,122.51 crore, RoAA 2.44%, capital adequacy 23.54%, and Tier I 23.07%. PBT rose due to higher AUM-driven NII and other income, partly offset by higher operating and credit costs; NIM fell to 5.24%. Gross NPA was ₹918.82 crore (2.27%) and net NPA ₹393.97 crore (0.98%). Business highlights note passenger car market growth of 1.87% and two-wheeler growth of 9.11%, with KMPL expanding operations, investing in technology, leveraging its branch network and distribution partnerships to capture vehicle demand while maintaining portfolio quality.

nodes.title: Leveraging technology to drive customer value and strengthening compliance
nodes.summary: KMPL used Aadhaar eKYC with facial recognition, data analytics, a cloud-based compliance platform, and a loan origination platform for Loan Against Property to improve efficiency, customer experience, and compliance. Kotak Mahindra Investments Limited (KMIL) focuses on real estate developer finance, corporate loans, and strategic investments. Financial highlights show net interest income of ₹606.85 crore, other income ₹188.00 crore, total income ₹794.85 crore, operating expenses ₹94.29 crore, provisions ₹26.05 crore, PBT ₹674.51 crore, PAT ₹501.25 crore, net customer assets ₹10,494.40 crore, RoAA 3.68%, capital adequacy 36.71%, Tier I 35.98%. PBT declined due to NPA provisions, lower processing fees, higher operating costs, offset by IPO income and provision reversal. Net customer assets decreased due to strong borrower performance. PAT fell 2.52%; NIM was 4.82%. Gross NPA ₹59.61 crore (0.59%), Net NPA ₹14.14 crore (0.14%).

nodes.title: A. Developing resilient technical infrastructure, platforms and cybersecurity frameworks
nodes.summary: The text details the Bank's resilient technical infrastructure and cybersecurity framework. It covers core infrastructure modernisation, including CBS enhancements, disaster recovery, and improved payment gateway and UPI performance. It describes unified digital platforms: Digital Banking Platform, Observability Platform, Unified Digital Onboarding Platform, Kotak AI Platform (including Koder and Kompanion), and Data EXchange (DEX) Platform. It outlines cybersecurity measures: 24x7 SOC, multi-factor authentication, encryption, application security, regulatory compliance (RBI, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, DPDP Act), and security culture. Finally, it mentions frontline digitisation initiatives like Transaction Authorisation System, reduced batch processing time, and an AI-powered bot.

nodes.title: b. Risk Management
nodes.summary:
b. Risk Management
The Bank analyses risk through machine learning models that continuously analyse transaction patterns, identifying anomalies that human reviewers might miss. This real-time risk assessment happens across millions of transactions daily, maintaining security without introducing friction into customer experiences.
The Bank’s monitoring infrastructure processes ~4 million metrics per minute, enabling deep visibility into system behaviour and potential risks. This massive data ingestion enables real-time fraud detection, automated compliance checks, dynamic risk scoring of customers based on behavioural patterns and external data sources and intelligent alert management.

nodes.title: c. Data Analytics
nodes.summary:
c. Data Analytics
The Bank has made substantial progress in advancing its data analytics capabilities by establishing a world-class team of data scientists and delivering solutions across a broad spectrum of use cases.
Data analytics has been integrated across the Bank’s operations to enhance risk underwriting through 360-degree customer profiling, deepen engagement through personalised offerings based on personas, transaction behaviour and external activity and strengthen fraud prevention by detecting and curbing mule activity.
To support these advancements, the data stack has been modernised with a build out of a new data platform and deployment of new machine learning-based decisioning systems for use cases across the business. This has enabled us to launch new models for underwriting, behaviour scores and a new predictive modelling framework to address customer service and complaints.

nodes.title: Kotak's Digital Apps and Platforms Overview
nodes.summary: The page describes Kotak's digital platforms—New Kotak Bank App, Kotak Cherry, Kotak811, Kotak Neo, and Kotak fyn—built on simplicity, speed, and security. The New Bank App serves affluent, non-resident, and self-employed customers with 250+ features, profile switching, one-click investments, EMI conversion, and biometric security. It outlines the Bank's future-ready ecosystem strategy. The Human Resources section details FY 2024-25 transformation: Group employee strength of ~114,100 and standalone 75,300; focus on employee experience and talent retention via Five Pillars of Talent Engagement, reducing attrition to 33.3% from 39.6%. nodes.title: Bank's Future Ecosystem, HR Transformation, and Employee Benefits
key_items: Building the Bank of Tomorrow, Today

nodes.title: Colleague Development

nodes.title: Building Appreciation and Transparent Communication at Kotak
key_items: Several initiatives were undertaken, such as:

It details Kotak Wonder Women initiatives, a Diversity and Inclusion Council, and women-focused policies: New Mother Benefit with flexible work and ₹7,500 monthly support, enhanced travel entitlements, Uber collaboration for safe travel, KWW Meet ALL networking, SheUnites sessions, and the ReLaunch second-career program. Emotional wellbeing and health coverage includes a 24x7 EAP, Annual Health Check screenings, specialised health camps, the Kotak Worklife App, and the Stepathon Challenge with 2,571 participants.

nodes.title: DEIB and Cultural Initiatives at the Bank
key_items: Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) Initiatives
nodes.summary: This page outlines the Bank's Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEIB) initiatives and cultural programs. It covers the Beyond Bias learning initiative that sensitized over 27,000 colleagues; the Am I an Inspiring Leader? programme for leadership accountability; the DRONA Coaching and Mentoring Program; training of over 2,800 Culture Drivers; and Customer-First Thinking workshops for about 8,500 leaders. It also details Kotak Wonder Women (KWW) initiatives, a Diversity and Inclusion Council, policies like the New Mother Benefit Policy and enhanced travel policies, collaboration with Uber for safe travel, KWW Meet ALL networking events, SheUnites sessions, and the Kotak ReLaunch Program for women returning to work.

nodes.title: Emotional Wellbeing and Health:
nodes.summary: The Bank links professional growth to personal wellbeing, highlighting the Employee Assistance Program for 24x7 confidential counseling. Preventive healthcare includes the Annual Health Check for eligible employees, discounted screenings for others, and specialized camps like breast cancer screenings and flu vaccinations. The Kotak Worklife App offers integrated access to health screenings, doctor consultations, telemedicine, and nutritionists. The Stepathon Challenge in December 2024 promoted physical activity with 2,571 participants, fostering personal fitness and collective wellness.

nodes.title: Employee Experience
nodes.summary: The text covers employee experience initiatives, including a seamless onboarding process and the Caring Kotakite volunteering program with 6,600 employees contributing 1,000 hours across 20 activities. It details the compliance framework, emphasizing regulatory adherence, a Board-approved New Products Approval Policy, compliance reviews, training, and monitoring. Internal controls are described through the Internal Audit department's risk-based approach, concurrent audits, and reporting lines. Risk management is outlined via the Enterprise-wide Risk Management framework, three lines of defence model, governance structure, roles of the CRO and committees, and the Group's AAA rating.

nodes.title: B. CAPITAL ADEQUACY
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Group's capital adequacy approach, covering active capital management driven by strategic needs and regulatory environment, maintaining a strong Tier I capital base for stability, growth, and competitive advantage. It details the balance between retaining capital and shareholder returns, an internal capital adequacy ratio with a discretionary cushion above regulatory minimums. It also covers the Leverage Ratio requirement, calculated using Basel III tier 1 capital and on/off-balance sheet items, and capital planning via a five-year ICAAP. Quarterly monitoring of capital utilization ensures buffers above requirements, with senior management considering capital implications in strategic decisions, and emphasis on maintaining capital above minimums, including under stress.

nodes.title: C. RISK APPETITE
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Group's risk appetite framework: Board-set top-down quantitative and qualitative statements defining acceptable risk for financial and strategic goals, establishing tone from the top, covering key risk factors, and enabling sustainable growth and stakeholder confidence. Cascaded to business segments with early triggers for proactive management, it is a key building block of risk culture and framework, linking risk to business and capital planning. Senior management reviews and recommends it to the Board for approval; annual plans are tested against it, exposures monitored regularly, and performance measured quarterly and reviewed by Senior Management, RMC, and Board, with actions to balance risk and return. The framework applies at consolidated and key legal entity levels.

nodes.title: D. CREDIT RISK
nodes.summary: The text covers credit risk as the Group's largest regulatory capital contributor, arising from customer or counterparty failure across wholesale, retail, off-balance sheet, and investment/trading portfolios. It details the top-down credit risk framework with policies and standards spanning the entire credit cycle, governance through delegated authorities and committees, and the credit philosophy emphasizing analysis, repayment capacity, and collateral. It differentiates wholesale lending (name-by-name, internal rating models, annual reviews) from retail lending (pool-based, scoring, product-specific guidelines). It outlines the three-stage credit process—pre-sanction (appraisal, rating), sanction (multi-level approval), and post-sanction (documentation, monitoring, independent loan review, early warning system, and recovery mechanisms).

nodes.title: E. COLLATERAL AND CREDIT RISK MITIGATION
nodes.summary: The text covers credit risk mitigation, starting with borrower assessment via financial and non-financial parameters. It details methods like facility structuring, collateral, guarantees, covenants, syndication, and loan assignments. It explains the Collateral management policy, including acceptable collateral types, valuation framework, haircuts based on risk, and periodic monitoring. Main collateral types are listed: cash, property, movable assets, inventory, receivables, and guarantees from higher-rated entities. It emphasizes legal enforceability, security verification, documentation, inspections, and timely registration by Credit Administration and Legal. Finally, it notes collateral release upon repayment or collection, subject to no other liens.

nodes.title: F. CREDIT RISK CONCENTRATION
nodes.summary: This section details the Bank's credit risk concentration management, covering portfolio and individual credit levels. It lists Board-approved limits for single/group borrowers, sectors, below investment grade accounts, country/bank exposures, and unsecured retail exposures, with internal limits tighter than regulatory norms. It describes monitoring against limits, actions for excess, use of loan sell-downs, and reporting to senior management. It mentions provisioning for stressed sectors above regulatory minimums, and monitoring of geographic locations, delinquency trends, facility types, and collaterals. It outlines the risk appetite mandate for diversification and periodic monitoring. It also covers the ICAAP under Pillar 2 for assessing additional capital for concentration risks and applying risk mitigation measures.

nodes.title: G. MARKET RISK IN TRADING BOOK
nodes.summary: The text defines market risk as potential economic loss from adverse changes in market risk factors like interest rates, foreign exchange rates, credit spreads, commodity and equity prices, and implied volatilities. It outlines governance through the Board-approved Investment Policy, Risk Management Committee, ALCO, Board Committee for Derivative Products, and Senior Management Committee for Derivatives. It details a comprehensive limit framework including sensitivity measures (PV01, Duration, Option Greeks), VaR limits, loss-triggers, value-limits, gap-limits, deal-size limits, tenor restrictions, and holding-period limits. The Market Risk Management unit reports to the Group Chief Risk Officer, ensuring identification, assessment, monitoring, and reporting, with intraday monitoring of major limits. It describes VaR methodology (historical simulation, 99% confidence, one-day holding period), back-testing, stress testing, and scenario analysis.

nodes.title: H. COUNTRY AND COUNTERPARTY CREDIT RISK
key_items: I. INTEREST RATE RISK IN BANKING BOOK (IRRBB)
nodes.summary: The text covers country risk, defined as loss from country-specific events like economic decline, political turmoil, nationalization, debt refusal, or currency depreciation, managed via a Board-approved policy with ALCO-approved limits. It discusses counterparty risk from financial institutions' obligations, with ALCO setting limits based on capital, asset quality, earnings, management, liquidity, etc. It explains pre-settlement risk quantification using market price and potential future exposure for regulatory capital, and settlement risk management via supervision or delivery-versus-payment. It notes regulatory initiatives for central counterparty (CCP) clearing of OTC derivatives to reduce systemic risk, with a dedicated CCP interface team and ALCO-approved CCP limits. It lists exposure management tools: counterparty selection, concentration limits, daily monitoring, escalation, pre-deal approvals, reporting, and stress testing. Finally, it covers interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB), including its sources from repricing mismatches, ALCO's policy role, BMU's management using funds transfer pricing, and risk measurement via earnings at risk and duration-based EVE sensitivity, with thresholds for NII and EVE.

nodes.title: J. LIQUIDITY RISK
nodes.summary: This text defines liquidity risk as the inability to meet obligations or finance asset growth without adverse financial impact or high costs. It covers the Group Liquidity policy, which maintains high-quality liquid assets and a diversified funding profile by source, instrument, term, and geography, with funding choices based on cost, market capacity, and stability. It details governance roles: ALCO defines strategy and tolerances, and BMU manages liquidity under a framework reviewed against regulatory and market changes. It explains internal funds transfer pricing, maturity-based interest rates, and limit-setting tools. Risk assessment uses structural and dynamic perspectives via stock, cash-flow, and stress-test approaches, plus prudential limits, cash-flow prediction models, back testing, and intra-day liquidity management. It describes scenario-based stress testing, LCR and NSFR requirements (both well above 100%), HQLA composition monitoring, and a Board-approved contingency liquidity plan with early warning indicators, governance, communication, and mitigation strategies.

nodes.title: K. OPERATIONAL RISK
nodes.summary: This text covers operational risk definition and management at a bank. It describes oversight by the Board, Risk Management Committee, and ORECs, plus IT security direction via the IT Risk and Information Security Committee and ARISTI awareness program. It explains the ORM framework, including RCSA, KRIs, and independent challenge, with internal audit and internal control oversight. Incident reporting, including near-misses, investigation, and disaster recovery/BCP testing are detailed. It outlines the Product and Process Approval Committee for new products, risk transfer via insurance, and the Board-approved Outsourcing policy aligned with RBI guidelines, including vendor risk assessment, scorecards, annual reviews, and monitoring of vendor audits and incidents.

nodes.title: L. FRAUD RISK
nodes.summary: This text defines fraud risk as the risk of financial loss and reputational damage from internal or external deceit, misrepresentation, or exploitation. It outlines the Bank's fraud risk management objectives, governance structure (Board, Risk Management Committee, SCBMF, Executive Committee), and centralized function guided by Board policy. It details preventive measures: Risk Containment Units, E-FRM system, unusual event framework, machine learning models, market intelligence, and Credit Monitoring Unit with early warning triggers. It covers whistleblower policy, staff accountability, internal reporting, third-party due diligence with accountability clauses, and regular audits. The text emphasizes cost-effective management within risk appetite, natural justice before fraud classification, and comprehensive oversight to prevent fraud and money laundering.

nodes.title: M. TECHNOLOGY RISKS
nodes.summary: The Bank manages technology risk through a layered architecture, disaster recovery, and BCP. It addresses end-of-life systems with planned upgrades, implements access controls with role-based provisioning and segregation of duties, and manages privileged access. A Cyber Resilience Framework mitigates threats like data breaches and malware. New digital products are assessed for cyber risks. Cyber drills, security monitoring, and incident response enhancements were conducted. Reviews covered ransomware and Microsoft 365 controls. The Bank monitors technology risk, regulatory requirements, and conducts audits/tests for control robustness, with continuous external threat monitoring.

nodes.title: N. REPUTATION RISK
nodes.summary: The text covers five risk management areas: Reputation Risk, emphasizing trust, sources of reputational damage, zero tolerance for inconsistent activities, and management via ERM policy and scorecard; Conduct Risk, addressing harm to consumers, market integrity, and competition, with mitigation through policies, culture, and HR practices, also assessed via scorecard; Risk Culture, focusing on accountability, communication, training, and embedding risk awareness in performance reviews and decision-making; ICAAP, describing annual assessment of Pillar II risks, capital adequacy, mitigation, and Board approval; and Stress Testing, as a key ICAAP tool for understanding portfolio performance under adverse conditions.

nodes.title: Conduct Risk, Risk Culture, and ICAAP Overview
key_items: Q. INTERNAL CAPITAL ADEQUACY ASSESSMENT PROCESS (‘ICAAP’)
nodes.summary: The page covers three sections: O. Conduct Risk, P. Risk Culture, and Q. ICAAP. Conduct Risk defines conduct risk, its sources, and the Bank’s framework for mitigation through policies, product approval, HR practices, and zero tolerance for misconduct, with assessment via an ICAAP scorecard. Risk Culture emphasizes desired attitudes and behaviors, governance, communication, training, and embedding risk management into performance reviews and business planning. ICAAP describes the annual process for assessing all significant risks (Pillar II), determining capital adequacy, risk mitigation, and Board approval, ensuring the Group is adequately capitalized.

nodes.title: R. STRESS TESTING
nodes.summary: The text covers stress testing within ICAAP, detailing its role in risk management, policy alignment, scenarios, liquidity tests, reverse stress testing, and reporting to management and Board. It also discusses pandemic, geopolitical, and tariff risks affecting the economy, and the Group's strong position. It references the Bank's business strategy, includes safe harbor statements about forward-looking statements and disclaimers, and notes regrouping of previous year figures.

nodes.title: Bank Stress Testing, Pandemic, Geopolitics, Tariffs and Business Strategy
key_items: S. PANDEMIC, GEO POLITICS AND TARIFFS
nodes.summary: The page covers the Bank's stress testing framework, including its Board-approved policy aligned with regulatory guidelines, covering material risks, liquidity stress tests, additional and reverse stress testing, and reporting to management and the Board. It notes stress test results inform risk appetite and business decisions, and that the Bank remained above capital ratios under all approved scenarios. The page also addresses pandemic-related disruptions, geopolitical risks like the Russia-Ukraine conflict and Middle East tensions, inflationary pressures, global interest rate fluctuations, US trade tensions and tariffs, and potential new trade restrictions, concluding the Group is well positioned to navigate the environment. It references the Bank's business strategy on pages 40-47.

nodes.title: SAFE HARBOUR
nodes.summary: The text covers a safe harbour statement with forward-looking statements subject to risks and uncertainties, including economic and political conditions, interest rate and market volatility, and regulatory changes. It clarifies the document is not an offer or recommendation for securities or financial products, which are subject to terms and conditions. It notes investment risks in mutual funds and securities, stating the sponsor's performance does not affect the mutual fund's performance. It details the Kotak Solitaire programme as invitation-only at the Bank's discretion, offering curated products and services via referrals and regulatory compliance. Finally, it mentions regrouped previous year figures.

It confirms an appeal has been preferred. It also lists regulatory agencies (Assistant Commissioner CGST Noida, Deputy Commissioner State Tax Ropar, Assistant Commissioner Central Tax Connaught Place) and references penalties/fines under Principle 1, along with report identifiers.

nodes.title: Brief of the Case
nodes.summary: The text details three GST orders received by a bank in August 2024 from tax authorities in Noida, Ropar, and New Delhi, each levying GST, interest under Section 50 of the CGST Act, and penalties under various sections. All demands stem from disallowed input tax credit for FY 2019-20. The orders include amounts: ₹16,14,944 GST plus ₹1,61,494 penalty; ₹4,49,864 GST plus ₹44,986 penalty; and ₹23,87,666 GST plus ₹2,38,767 penalty. Appeals have been preferred for all. Additionally, it lists regulatory agencies (Deputy Commissioner of State Tax, Mazgaon, Mumbai; Office of the Principal Commissioner of Central Tax, Hyderabad) and mentions NGRBC Principle 1 penalties/fines.

The second, from Hyderabad, levies GST of ₹4,89,648 plus interest and a penalty of ₹68,756 for FY 2019-20, mainly for input tax credit disallowance. Appeals have been preferred for both. It notes appeals were preferred for all three orders and lists regulatory agencies and monetary amounts, including NGRBC Principle 1 penalties.

nodes.title: Scope of Work and Boundary
nodes.summary: The text outlines the scope and boundary of an assurance engagement for KMBL's BRSR disclosures for FY 2024-25, covering reasonable assurance for BRSR Core indicators and limited assurance for remaining non-financial disclosures. It details specific boundaries for BRSR Core attributes: GHG footprint (India locations), water footprint (40 key corporate offices), and circularity/waste management (40 key corporate offices, excluding e-waste and C&D waste reported for all India locations). Limited assurance covers India operations and two international branches. Reporting criteria include SEBI circulars, GHG Protocol, and ISO 14064-1:2018. The assurance methodology follows DNV's VeriSustainTM protocol and ISAE 3000, with activities like system evaluation, stakeholder engagement, and on-site audits. Inherent limitations include ±5% materiality, reliance on third-party audited financial data for certain attributes, and exclusions such as future statements and strategy review.

nodes.title: Assurance Methodology and Basis for BRSR Disclosures
key_items: Assurance Methodology/Standard and Level of Assurance
nodes.summary: The page outlines DNV's assurance methodology using the VeriSustainTM protocol and ISAE 3000, detailing reasonable assurance for BRSR Core KPIs under 9 ESG attributes and limited assurance for other non-financial disclosures. The basis of conclusion describes activities for both assurance levels: for BRSR Core, review of disclosures, evaluation of systems and controls, extensive evidence gathering, stakeholder engagement, and on-site audits at selected sites based on contribution, complexity, and reporting systems, with sites listed in Annexure II. For limited assurance, review of general disclosures, management processes, principle-wise performance, and other metrics; understanding systems, sample-based testing, documentary evidence evaluation, and risk-based on-site audits at corporate offices and sites. Both include interviews with senior managers and verification of consolidated performance for completeness.

nodes.title: Inherent Limitations
nodes.summary: The text outlines the inherent limitations of DNV's assurance engagement, assuming data provided by the Company is in good faith, true, complete, sufficient, authentic, and free from material misstatements. Limitations include: a ±5% uncertainty based on materiality threshold for estimation/measurement errors and omissions; DNV not evaluating financial data or performance, with reliance on third-party audited financial reports for specific BRSR Core Attributes and indicators involving currency, disclaiming responsibility for financial data; assessment limited to the defined Reporting Period; exclusion of data outside specified operations; exclusion of statements expressing opinions, claims, beliefs, aspirations, expectations, aims, or future intentions, as well as Intellectual Property Rights and competitive issues; no review of strategy or related linkages; no mapping to reporting frameworks other than those specified; exclusion of aspects outside the mentioned scope and boundary; and no review of legal compliances, with the Company responsible for legal adherence.

nodes.title: Responsibility of the Company
nodes.summary:
Responsibility of the Company
Use and distribution of Assurance statement
KMBL has the sole responsibility for the preparation of the BRSR and is responsible for all information disclosed in the BRSR Core and BRSR. The company is responsible for maintaining processes and procedures for collecting, analyzing and reporting the information and also, ensuring the quality and consistency of the information presented in the Report. KMBL is also responsible for ensuring the maintenance and integrity of its website and any referenced BRSR disclosures on their website.

nodes.title: DNV’s Responsibility
nodes.summary: The text outlines DNV's responsibility in assurance work, stating accountability to company management while providing independent opinion for stakeholders, and disclaiming liability for decisions based on the statement. It includes digital signatures of Chandan Sarkar (Lead Verifier) and Anjana Sharma (Assurance Reviewer), the assurance team members, date and location (07/07/2025, Bengaluru, India), company name DNV Business Assurance India Private Limited, statement number DNV-2025-ASR-788271-1, and references the Integrated Annual Report 2024-25, annexures, assurance statements, and page number.

It references the independent assurance statement by DNV for Kotak Mahindra Bank's FY2024-25 Integrated Report, covering scope (limited assurance for non-financial performance per GRI standards; reasonable assurance for energy, water, emissions, waste), reporting criteria (GRI 2021, IIRC, SEBI BRSR, GHG Protocol), methodology (VeriSustain, ISAE 3000, ISO 14064-3, ISO 14046), basis of conclusion (risk-based approach, evidence collection, adherence to principles), responsibilities of KMBL and DNV, use and distribution restrictions, assured GRI disclosures, and statement number DNV-2025-ASR-788271-2.

nodes.title: Location
nodes.summary: The text is an assurance statement annexure listing audit sites: Corporate Office Mumbai, India sites onsite and remote including Mumbai, Noida, and Delhi. DNV Business Assurance India conducted an independent assurance of Kotak Mahindra Bank's sustainability disclosures in its FY2024-25 Integrated Report. It details the scope: limited assurance for non-financial performance based on GRI standards, with reasonable assurance for specific GRI indicators on energy, water, emissions, and waste, covering global operations. Reporting criteria include GRI 2021, IIRC framework, SEBI BRSR, and GHG Protocol. The methodology uses DNV's VeriSustain protocol, ISAE 3000, ISO 14064-3, and ISO 14046. nodes.title: Independent Assurance Statement for KMBL Integrated Report FY2024-25
key_items: to the Management of Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited
nodes.summary: The page is an independent assurance statement by DNV for Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited's sustainability disclosures in its Integrated Report for FY 2024-25. It covers: the engagement and independence of DNV; scope and boundary, including limited assurance for non-financial performance based on GRI Topic-specific Standards and reasonable assurance for specified GRI indicators (Energy, Water, Emissions, Waste) also disclosed in BRSR, covering global operations under direct control; reporting criteria and standards (GRI Standards 2021, IIRC Framework, SEBI BRSR, GHG Protocol); and assurance methodology using DNV's VeriSustainTM protocol (V6.0), ISAE 3000 (revised), ISO 14064-3, and ISO 14046.

nodes.title: Basis of our conclusion
nodes.summary: The text is an assurance statement from DNV Business Assurance India Private Limited regarding KMBL's Integrated Annual Report 2024-25. It details the basis of conclusion, including a risk-based approach, review of disclosures, understanding of systems and controls, walk-throughs, evidence collection, on-site audits, interviews, and verification of performance disclosures against the VeriSustainTM Protocol. It assesses adherence to principles of Materiality, Responsiveness, Reliability/Accuracy, Completeness, and Neutrality/Balance, concluding that nothing came to attention suggesting misstatement. It outlines responsibilities of KMBL and DNV, use and distribution of the statement, and includes signatures and assurance team details.

Responsibility of the Company
KMBL has the sole responsibility for the preparation of the Report and is responsible for all information disclosed in the Report. The company is responsible for maintaining processes and procedures for collecting, analyzing and reporting the information and ensuring the quality and consistency of the information presented in the Report. KMBL is also responsible for ensuring the maintenance and integrity of its website and any referenced disclosures on their website.
DNV’s Responsibility
In performing this assurance work, DNV’s responsibility is to the Management of the Company; however, this statement represents our independent opinion and is intended to inform the outcome of the assurance to the stakeholders of the Company. DNV disclaims any liability or co-responsibility for any decision a person or entity would make based on this assurance statement.

nodes.summary: The notice section covers Kotak Mahindra Bank's 40th AGM on August 2, 2025, via video conferencing, including ordinary business: adoption of financial statements, dividend declaration, reappointment of Ms. Shanti Ekambaram and Mr. Ashok Vaswani as Directors, and appointment of M M Nissim & Co LLP as Joint Statutory Auditors.
